Ecov aims at tackling this lack of affordable and flexible mobility solution outside of city centres. Its concept is based on connected carpooling stations that match drivers in their local car use with passengers looking for a flexible and cost-saving journey. ... drivers do not need to register, nor do they need to commit to a particular itinerary or schedule. record.text: How are EU-funded projects turning the everyday car journeys that local residents already make into a bookable service for other travellers, so that thinly populated places with too few passengers to support frequent scheduled services still get a usable connection to the wider transport network?
record.reference_answer: Three projects treat the trips residents already drive as the missing service in places too thinly settled for frequent scheduled transport. LOCARP4EU assesses Ecov's roadside carpooling stations, in which street terminals, road signs and an IT system handling payment pair local drivers with waiting passengers without the driver having to register or commit to an itinerary or schedule, aimed at city outskirts and the remote fringes local authorities struggle to serve; it puts the locally carpoolable share at 5% of total passenger-kilometres. RIDE2RAIL makes shared rides a complementary mode that extends rail and public transport networks, harmonising real-time information on rail, public transport, ride-sharing and crowdsourcing behind Travel Companion features and a crowd-based Transport Service Provider, explicitly to reinforce offers in rural and low-demand areas and open access to high-capacity services, tested in Padua, Athens, Brno and Helsinki. UNITE scales the Karos platform, which applies artificial intelligence to turn empty car seats into low-cost public-transport-like networks in low density areas, claiming a network extension and densification by a factor of 10 and a transport cost divided by 10, and sold as Karos Territories to local transportation authorities and Karos Enterprise to companies.

Reading the texts showed 101034449 CLOE is a doctoral programme on mountain/rural sustainable development whose only 'mobility' is MSCA mobility rules - a tag/LIKE false positive, dropped. The corpus-wide theme was narrowed to the mechanism that two of the seeds' texts actually describe (matching private drivers' existing journeys with passengers in poorly served low-density areas) so that the gold set is decidable. Pooled search on the final question text (k=10, all four conditions, 25 distinct projects). IN: 762399 LOCARP4EU (Ecov connected carpooling stations matching drivers 'in their local car use' with passengers, targeting 'cities' outskirts' with 'less developed public transport networks' and authorities' 'remote fringes'); 881825 RIDE2RAIL (ride sharing as 'a complementary transport mode that extends public transport and rail networks ... especially in rural and low-demand areas'); 954654 UNITE (Karos: 'transform empty car seats into sustainable and low-cost-to-operate public transportation networks in low density areas', extending the public transportation network). OUT with reasons: 770115 INCLUSION - broad accessibility assessment and pilot catalogue for vulnerable users, does not build a service from residents' own car trips; 757004 BUSUP - crowd-sourced bus bookings with bus operators, suburban/exurban and events; 745016 SHOTL and 769033 AVENUE - operator-run on-demand shuttles/autonomous minibuses, not private cars; 726547 GoOpti - long-distance DRT with professional drivers to airports; 636427 SocialCar - carpooling explicitly 'in urban and peri-urban areas', validated at 10 European urban sites, no thin-service framing; 744972 KAROS - intra-city commuting carpooling with employers, Paris region; 699017 TAG - carpooling for cities; 769513 STARS, 735385 MobiCS, 762543 iShare, 775417 P2PCS, 791958 ECCOCAR - vehicle sharing/rental, not shared rides in low-density areas; 769819 HiReach - transport-poverty incubator funding startups across many service concepts rather than operating one; 762220 TownHall24 - platform for access to municipal services; 800267 ECOINTELS - economic modelling of demand-responsive services; 713626 SOM - travel-intention prediction app; 687959 CROWD4ROADS - BlaBlaCar plus road-surface crowd sensing, goal is occupancy and road monitoring; 826385 MaaSive, 730846 Co-Active, 826252 Shift2MaaS, 636126 ETC, 635867 BONVOYAGE, 636148 EuTravel, 723176 MaaS4EU, 878052 MAAS - ticketing/MaaS/journey-planning platforms; 875588 TRIPS, 723194 Cities-4-People, 955332 SCALE-UP, 689031 DESTINATIONS, 870753 SMARTDEST, 101006853 FastTrack, 956030 TOD-IS-RUR, 835197 ViAjeRo, 769606 CAMERA, 640353 DATASET2050, 635885 DORA, 636012 ELIPTIC, 690650 SUITS, 777640 My-TRAC, 881791 FINE-2, 777627 SMaRTE, 778764 SIADE SaaS, 696935 D3IMPACT, 683765 OPTEPLA, 787674 DRIVER GLASS, 815003 Trustonomy, 780371 FABULOS, 683366 ParkBee, 729640 SMART BIKING, 729619 PAL, 703047 SuMAC, 671566 SUPERFLUIDITY, 778533 Home2nite - off-topic or urban transport with no residents'-own-journeys mechanism. record.text: How are EU-funded projects turning the everyday car journeys that local residents already make into a bookable service for other travellers, so that thinly populated places with too few passengers to support frequent scheduled services still get a usable connection to the wider transport network?
record.reference_answer: Four projects treat the trips residents already drive as the missing service in places too thinly settled for frequent scheduled transport. LOCARP4EU assesses Ecov's roadside carpooling stations, in which street terminals, road signs and an IT system handling payment pair local drivers with waiting passengers without the driver having to register or commit to an itinerary or schedule, aimed at city outskirts and the remote fringes local authorities struggle to serve; it puts the locally carpoolable share at 5% of total passenger-kilometres. RIDE2RAIL makes shared rides a complementary mode that extends rail and public transport networks, harmonising real-time information on rail, public transport, ride-sharing and crowdsourcing behind Travel Companion features and a crowd-based Transport Service Provider, explicitly to reinforce offers in rural and low-demand areas and open access to high-capacity services, tested in Padua, Athens, Brno and Helsinki. Two successive projects of the same firm cover the two ends of that idea: the earlier KAROS feasibility project tuned carpooling to short-distance trips and mixed carpooling lines with mass transit lines into what it calls a new, efficient public transportation system, reporting more than 40.000 carpool trips and 244 low density towns reconnected to the mass transit system, while the later UNITE scales the platform, applying artificial intelligence to turn empty car seats into low-cost public-transport-like networks in low density areas, claiming a network extension and densification by a factor of 10 and a transport cost divided by 10, sold as Karos Territories to local transportation authorities and Karos Enterprise to companies.

record.text: How do the aims differ between projects that study the woodwork of ships that sank centuries ago - what does each team hope those old ship timbers can tell them?
record.reference_answer: Both projects read the wood of ships that went down centuries ago, but they ask opposite kinds of question of it. ModernShip Project works on the structural remains of 16th-century wrecks of Mediterranean build - Mortella (1527, France) and Santiago de Galicia (1597, Spain), alongside the already documented Lomellina and Calvi I - in order to draft, for the first time, a Mediterranean technical model of how such ships were put together and to set it against the better-known Atlantic one, so that the continuous exchanges and technological transfers between the two nautical spaces can be described. TIMBER treats ship timber instead as precisely dated evidence about a resource: tree-ring work on the Swedish warship Vasa, built in Stockholm in 1628 and sunk on her first voyage in Stockholm Harbour, confirmed timbers from at least four distinct sources, including a Baltic and a west Swedish source, alongside purchase records naming eastern Sweden, Riga, Koenigsberg and Amsterdam, showing that even in heavily forested Sweden timber was imported from abroad. On the Boele Ship, a wreck dated to the 1380s found in the river Skienselva in southern Norway that sank with a cargo of whetstones from Eidsborg, every timber analysed - the keel included - came from the southern Baltic around the mouth of the Vistula River, which TIMBER reads not as evidence for the transport of timber but as a ship built at the Vistula mouth; both cases feed its account of the maritime timber trade from c. AD 1100 to 1700, with felling dates and regions of origin. The difference is what the wood is evidence for: for ModernShip it is evidence of design and construction practice in two coexisting technical cultures, for TIMBER it is evidence of where trees were felled, who traded them and how timber moved.

record.text: What separation-management approaches for drone traffic have European U-space projects developed themselves - their own methods for keeping drones apart and resolving conflicts - as opposed to demonstrating separation services supplied by others?

pooling_evidence.note: single pooled run at k=40 over the final wording; 57 distinct pooled projects = 9 accepted-from-pool + 48 rejected. 776293 GAUSS is gold but retrieved by no condition at k=40; its provenance is the completeness sweep, recorded here rather than folded into the pooled arithmetic. hybrid_rerank returns 20 projects (reranker stage cap), the other three conditions 40.

record.reference_answer: European work on U-space separation splits between designing the separation service itself and validating deconfliction technology in flight. BUBBLES formulates a U-Space advanced (U3) separation management service at TRL3, computing UAS collision risk so that separation minima and methods - procedural, tactical self-separated or tactical ground-based - can be derived from a stated probability of collision. USEPE studies separation methods for demanding environments such as cities and applies machine learning to automate safe separation and deconfliction while holding airspace capacity. Metropolis 2 treats airspace design, flight planning and separation management as interdependent at high traffic density, comparing concepts that differ in how separation is performed (strategic/tactical, ground/air) by simulation before a real-world demonstration, while DACUS embeds separation management in a Demand and Capacity Balancing process and searches for the optimal balance between on-board separation intelligence and U-space separation service intelligence. LABYRINTH takes the centralised route, computing 4D paths for drone swarms so trajectories do not collide. On the technology and demonstration side, CLASS matured ground-based tracking with tactical deconfliction tools that suggest new conflict-free trajectories; IMPETUS tested tactical de-confliction in which virtual weights attached to each drone define the separation criteria, giving dynamic separation; TINDAiR demonstrated AI-based tactical deconfliction with a detect-and-avoid service over VTOL flights; GOF2.0 validated an architecture for highly automated real-time separation assurance in dense urban airspace; and GAUSS approaches coordination among UAS through Galileo-EGNOS precise positioning plus tactical deconfliction services in its UTM system.
record.notes: Membership criterion is now STATED IN THE QUESTION: a project is gold iff its own stored text shows it developed or validated its own method for keeping drones apart or resolving conflicts between them (separation minima, strategic or tactical deconfliction, conflict detection and resolution) within U-space/UTM; a project that only demonstrates or consumes a separation-type service supplied by partners is excluded by the question's own words ('as opposed to demonstrating separation services supplied by others'), as is on-board sensing hardware and manned-aviation separation work. The earlier 'large numbers of drones' qualifier was dropped because gold members TINDAiR (largest exercise: 'Deconfliction between an autonomous drone, an eVTOL carrying a passenger and a manned helicopter') and GAUSS ('4 UTM coordinated RPAS') do not satisfy it. IN (10): 890378 USEPE ('research on drones' separation methods in high demanding environments such as cities', ML for separation and deconfliction); 892928 Metropolis 2 (unified approach to airspace design and separation management; strategic/tactical deconfliction, dynamic capacity management; compares its own separation concepts by simulation); 893206 BUBBLES (formulation and validation of a U3 separation management service, own collision-risk algorithms, separation minima and methods); 893864 DACUS (own DCB process integrating separation management, on-board vs U-space separation intelligence); 861696 LABYRINTH (own centralized 4D path-planning system computing paths to avoid collisions for drone swarms under U-SPACE); 101017677 TINDAiR (own AI-based tactical deconfliction demonstrated in flight, Tactical Conflict Resolution and DAA); 101017689 GOF2.0 (own GOF 2.0 architecture for highly automated real-time separation assurance; trials driven by strategic deconfliction); 763719 CLASS (own ground-based UTMS with tactical deconfliction - 'Airbus teams investigated deconfliction by adapting available algorithms from manned aviation. The traffic simulator and the conflict detection have been tuned to drone characteristics'); 763807 IMPETUS (own tactical de-confliction concept tested, virtual weights defining separation criteria for dynamic separation); 776293 GAUSS (objective: 'coordination among a higher number of RPAS' and 'the definition, negotiation and execution of safe trajectories'; finalResults: 'Development of algorithms and functionalities for U-space in-flight services ... such as UTM simulators and tactical deconfliction services' - mechanism is Galileo/EGNOS positioning rather than a separation algorithm, which the reference states). Demonstrator cases resolved explicitly under the stated criterion, all OUT: 783230 PODIUM (self-described 'U-Space compliant demonstration'; its finalResults report evidence on partners' services 'including drone registration and identification, automatic flight plan validation ... and conflict detection and alerting' - it evaluates services it did not develop); 101017701 SAFIR-Med ('leveraged to make use of the maximum number of U-Space services ..., including advanced Detect And Avoid U-space service'); 101017682 CORUS-XUAM (VLD campaigns in which 'Vertiport procedures, separation, and data services will be also demonstrated' using partners' U-space deployments); 101017643 Uspace4UAM (VLD demonstrations with 'a well experienced UTM provider'); 783261 USIS (demonstrates a list of initial U-space services - e-identification, tracking, flight planning, monitoring). record.text: What have EU-funded research projects learned about how the judges at the global courts that put individuals on trial for the gravest crimes of war and mass violence understand their own role in shaping the law through their rulings?
record.reference_answer: Two projects speak to this. INCRICO interviewed judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and found that they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law: they also treat fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, case management and governance - and, to a lesser degree, protecting the interests and values of the international community - as part of their judicial function, and these self-understandings feed back into the Court's deliberations, the drafting of its judgments and its use of separate and dissenting opinions. EaRL asked the same question of the wider international criminal bench, combining a systematic reading of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts (the ICC, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL)) with over 40 in-depth interviews with judges, civil-society staff and government representatives, and traced empirically how routine practices of legal interpretation come to produce new legal meaning. Taken together, the two projects describe a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements, and both look outward as well - INCRICO at how the Court's judgments are received as authoritative, EaRL at how a wider interpretive community of government officials, NGOs and other international courts takes up those decisions.

record.text: What have EU-funded research projects learned about how the judges at the global courts that put individuals on trial for the gravest crimes of war and mass violence understand their own role in shaping the law through their rulings?
record.reference_answer: Two projects speak to this. INCRICO interviewed judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and found that they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law: they also treat fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, case management and governance - and, to a lesser degree, protecting the interests and values of the international community - as part of their judicial function, and these self-understandings feed back into the Court's deliberations, the drafting of its judgments and its use of separate and dissenting opinions. EaRL asked the same question of the wider international criminal bench, combining a systematic reading of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts (the ICC, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL)) with over 40 in-depth interviews with judges, civil-society staff and government representatives, and traced empirically how routine practices of legal interpretation come to produce new legal meaning. Taken together, the two projects describe a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements, and both look outward as well - INCRICO at how the Court's judgments are received as authoritative, EaRL at how a wider interpretive community of government officials, NGOs and other international courts takes up those decisions.

The overall goal is to offer a realistic account of the international criminal judiciary with regard to judicial deliberations, reasoning and drafting judgments. ... (2) gather (through in-depth interviews with the ICC's judges) and analyse qualitative data on the judges' perceptions and understanding of their judicial function, in terms of what and how the judges really think, and what they are doing and why ..."
- report summary, verbatim: "It examines how ICC judges themselves view their jobs and cope with difficult legal issues in complex criminal cases, and how judicial understandings of their role influence the actual practices and decisions of the Court. ... - report finalResults, verbatim: "Extended interviews with ICC judges provide unique empirical material on the experience and dilemmas of the men and women on the international criminal bench. The interviews suggest that ICC judges' perceptions of their duties go well beyond the idea that courts should apply existing, recognised rules/principles of law to the questions before them. record.text: What have EU-funded research projects learned about how the judges at the global courts that put individuals on trial for the gravest crimes of war and mass violence understand their own role in shaping the law through their rulings?
record.reference_answer: Two projects speak to this. INCRICO interviewed judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and found that they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law: they also treat fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, case management and governance - and, to a lesser degree, protecting the interests and values of the international community - as part of their judicial function, and these self-understandings feed back into the Court's deliberations, the drafting of its judgments and its use of separate and dissenting opinions. EaRL asked the same question of the wider international criminal bench, combining a systematic reading of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts (the ICC, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL)) with over 40 in-depth interviews with judges, civil-society staff and government representatives, and traced empirically how routine practices of legal interpretation come to produce new legal meaning. Taken together, the two projects describe a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements, and both look outward as well - INCRICO at how the Court's judgments are received as authoritative, EaRL at how a wider interpretive community of government officials, NGOs and other international courts takes up those decisions.

- report finalResults, verbatim: "Extended interviews with ICC judges provide unique empirical material on the experience and dilemmas of the men and women on the international criminal bench. The interviews suggest that ICC judges' perceptions of their duties go well beyond the idea that courts should apply existing, recognised rules/principles of law to the questions before them. record.text: What have EU-funded research projects learned about how the judges at the global courts that put individuals on trial for the gravest crimes of war and mass violence understand their own role in shaping the law through their rulings?
record.reference_answer: Two projects speak to this. INCRICO interviewed judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and found that they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law: they also treat fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, case management and governance - and, to a lesser degree, protecting the interests and values of the international community - as part of their judicial function, and these self-understandings feed back into the Court's deliberations, the drafting of its judgments and its use of separate and dissenting opinions. EaRL asked the same question of the wider international criminal bench, combining a systematic reading of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts (the ICC, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL)) with over 40 in-depth interviews with judges, civil-society staff and government representatives, and traced empirically how routine practices of legal interpretation come to produce new legal meaning. Taken together, the two projects describe a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements, and both look outward as well - INCRICO at how the Court's judgments are received as authoritative, EaRL at how a wider interpretive community of government officials, NGOs and other international courts takes up those decisions.

evidence:
Gold 746768 INCRICO - "The International Criminal Court and the Judicial Function: a Socio-Legal Study of Judicial Perceptions and Practices"
- objective, verbatim: "INCRICO investigates the ways in which the International Criminal Court (ICC) perceives its judicial function and how this impacts its legal practices. The overall goal is to offer a realistic account of the international criminal judiciary with regard to judicial deliberations, reasoning and drafting judgments. ... (2) gather (through in-depth interviews with the ICC's judges) and analyse qualitative data on the judges' perceptions and understanding of their judicial function, in terms of what and how the judges really think, and what they are doing and why ..."
- report summary, verbatim: "It examines how ICC judges themselves view their jobs and cope with difficult legal issues in complex criminal cases, and how judicial understandings of their role influence the actual practices and decisions of the Court. ... First, to examine the inner (deliberative) process, the drafting process and the functions ICC judges ascribe to their work, including the use of separate and dissenting opinions."
- report finalResults, verbatim: "Extended interviews with ICC judges provide unique empirical material on the experience and dilemmas of the men and women on the international criminal bench. The interviews suggest that ICC judges' perceptions of their duties go well beyond the idea that courts should apply existing, recognised rules/principles of law to the questions before them. They reveal that ICC judges see additional objectives as part of the ICC's judicial function, including fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, managing cases and governance."

Gold 748114 EaRL - "Expert Rule? Judges, Lawyers, and the Practices of Interpretation in International Criminal Law"
- objective, verbatim: "At the same time, international judges have begun to change and potentially even create law through their decisions. In international criminal law, a particularly drastic example, international judges repeatedly described the development of international criminal law as one of their main achievements. ... EaRL is based on a systematic analysis of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts, including the International Criminal Court, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL). In addition, it uses over 40 in-depth expert interviews with international judges, staff at civil society organisations, and government representatives."
- report finalResults, verbatim: "Relying on legal theory, it analyzed and traced empirically how the practices of legal interpretation can lead to the development of legal meaning. ... The project investigated empirically how a broader interpretive community including government officials and staff at non-governmental organizations and other international and internationalized courts engages with these judgements to inquire into the broader relevance of these decisions."

It fills the vector route's under-filled paraphrase axis and adds a social-sciences/law domain the vector entries do not yet cover. L2 synthesis is honest by count and by shape: exactly two projects in 35,389 satisfy it, and neither answers alone - INCRICO supplies the ICC judges' own account of their function, EaRL supplies the cross-court evidence that interpretive practice develops the law.

findings.claim: Gold member 748114 (EaRL) answers the 'shaping the law through their rulings' half of the question but not the 'how the judges understand their own role' half; its only statement of judges' self-understanding is a background premise, not a project finding. findings.evidence: Full read of 748114 via get_project_text. Its finalResults lists five results, verbatim: (1) 'analyzed and traced empirically how the practices of legal interpretation can lead to the development of legal meaning'; (2) 'investigated empirically how a broader interpretive community including government officials and staff at non-governmental organizations and other international and internationalized courts engages with these judgements'; (3) a methodological toolbox; (4) a contribution to the IR 'practice turn'; (5) the basis for an ICTY/ECtHR citation-network project. None reports what judges think their role is. Its workPerformed says the judge interviews were run 'to gain new empirical insights into the broader relevance of the decisions of international criminal courts, and how the legal authority of these courts is constructed' - reception and authority, not self-perception. The single self-understanding sentence, 'international judges repeatedly described the development of international criminal law as one of their main achievements', is the objective's framing of prior observation, and the summary immediately turns it into the question EaRL tests ('But have these courts been able to deliver on this objective?'). The draft's own reference answer reproduces the gap: every clause that answers the question as asked ('they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law', the fact-finding/law-making/governance list) is quoted from INCRICO's finalResults, while the EaRL clauses describe the 240 judgements, the interviews, and the interpretive community; the bridging sentence 'a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements' rests on EaRL's background line, not on any EaRL result.

The reference answer's 'taken together' sentence would need to stop attributing the self-description to both projects.

record.text: What have EU-funded research projects learned about how the judges at the global courts that put individuals on trial for the gravest crimes of war and mass violence understand their own role in shaping the law through their rulings?
record.reference_answer: Two projects speak to this. INCRICO interviewed judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and found that they see their duties as going well beyond applying recognised rules of law: they also treat fact-finding, dispute settlement, law-making, case management and governance - and, to a lesser degree, protecting the interests and values of the international community - as part of their judicial function, and these self-understandings feed back into the Court's deliberations, the drafting of its judgments and its use of separate and dissenting opinions. EaRL asked the same question of the wider international criminal bench, combining a systematic reading of all 240 available judgements of international criminal and hybrid courts (the ICC, the ad hoc Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and Rwanda (ICTR), and the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL)) with over 40 in-depth interviews with judges, civil-society staff and government representatives, and traced empirically how routine practices of legal interpretation come to produce new legal meaning. Taken together, the two projects describe a bench that regards developing the law as one of its own achievements, and both look outward as well - INCRICO at how the Court's judgments are received as authoritative, EaRL at how a wider interpretive community of government officials, NGOs and other international courts takes up those decisions.

findings.evidence: Full read of 748114 via get_project_text. Its finalResults lists five results, verbatim: (1) 'analyzed and traced empirically how the practices of legal interpretation can lead to the development of legal meaning'; (2) 'investigated empirically how a broader interpretive community including government officials and staff at non-governmental organizations and other international and internationalized courts engages with these judgements'; (3) a methodological toolbox; (4) a contribution to the IR 'practice turn'; (5) the basis for an ICTY/ECtHR citation-network project. None reports what judges think their role is. Its workPerformed says the judge interviews were run 'to gain new empirical insights into the broader relevance of the decisions of international criminal courts, and how the legal authority of these courts is constructed' - reception and authority, not self-perception. The single self-understanding sentence, 'international judges repeatedly described the development of international criminal law as one of their main achievements', is the objective's framing of prior observation, and the summary immediately turns it into the question EaRL tests ('But have these courts been able to deliver on this objective?'). record.text: Some EU projects build solar-fuel photoelectrodes out of carbon nitride rather than a metal-based semiconductor, so they have to work out how to make the material themselves. How do those projects differ in the routes they use to produce and deposit the carbon nitride layer?
record.reference_answer: MFreePEC works bottom-up from the molecule: it encodes the composition of a family of metal-free CNX materials (X = P, B or S) into supramolecular precursors, uses the stable intermediate melem to synthesise CN photoanodes in the 5-20 min range at higher temperatures, and gets the layer onto transparent conductive electrodes by electrophoretic deposition, ultrasonic spray of precursors, doctor-blading, dip-coating and added precursor vapour pressure during calcination - a porous carbon-nitride photoanode containing reduced graphene oxide and a nickel-iron oxyhydroxide oxidation co-catalyst held photocurrents exceeding 0.45 mA/cm2 at 1.23 V vs. NHE for more than 35 h. CALSOL instead pits two whole synthesis routes against each other for its carbon-based artificial leaf - the traditional thermal polycondensation route and a plasma polymerization route - and its headline result is negative about the traditional one: the product of thermal polycondensation of melamine is not graphitic carbon nitride but a defective melon structure that degraded considerably during photoelectrochemical experiments, with a flatband potential drifting from approx. -1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl to -1.8 vs. Ag/AgCl across pH. The contrast is therefore between engineering precursor chemistry and deposition method to build a durable working photoanode (MFreePEC) and testing whether an established preparation route yields a usable carbon nitride photoelectrode material at all (CALSOL).
record.notes: Seeds: 849068 MFreePEC and 797781 CALSOL, the only two projects whose text shows carbon nitride itself being made and deposited as the photoactive layer of a solar-fuel photoelectrode. Pooled k=10, 19 candidates, 2 accepted. Adjudications - IN: 797781 CALSOL (two carbon nitride synthesis routes tried: thermal polycondensation and plasma polymerization; photoelectrode stability and flatband potential measured), 849068 MFreePEC (controlled synthesis/growth of CNX layers, five deposition techniques onto transparent conductive electrodes, CN photoanodes). OUT: 883264 Sun-To-X (photoelectrode support of FTO-coated quartz felt, inorganic-oxide photoanode/polymer photocathode, no carbon nitride anywhere in its text); 745604 CO2RED (carbon nitride used as a bought-in light-harvester for suspension photocatalysts; the photoelectrode it actually built was p-doped silicon with a mesoporous titania layer and an immobilized cobalt phthalocyanine - it develops no route to produce or deposit carbon nitride); 861151 SOLAR2CHEM (ITN; finalResults claims 'fabrication for the first time of photoelectrode-based carbon nitrides' but its text describes no synthesis or deposition route - borderline, and even if counted IN the level stays L2); 864234 SECANS (transition metal nitride semiconductors - metal-based, the contrast the question draws); 850624 THEIA (porous boron nitride, not carbon nitride); 732840 A-LEAF (metal/metal-oxide catalysts); 101022649 METHASOL (g-CN as an OER photocatalyst in a MOF Z-scheme for gas-phase CO2 reduction; the word photoelectrode/photoanode/photocathode/photoelectrochemical never appears in its text); 715354 p-TYPE, 716539 HybridSolarFuels, 793996 CO2SPLITTING, 654723 Solarfuels, 749231 CO2 Intermediates, 895296 RENEW, 101024839 PHOTOBIOCATH-CO2, 644013 CREATe-Network, 796388 ECOMAT (none contains carbon nitride/C3N4 in any indexed chunk); 101031365 SolTIME (carbon nitride named in the objective only, as the platform copper porphyrins are interfaced to; no synthesis or deposition of the material). record.text: Which projects study the workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces, such as couriers, drivers, or people paid task by task over the internet?
record.reference_answer: Eight projects study this workforce, in three groups. Fieldwork on who these workers are and what the work does to them: PLABOR established that platform-based gig work in Amsterdam, Berlin and New York City is predominantly migrant work and documents the new risks it creates; GHOSTWORK follows the people who clean, code and classify data for AI on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, who cannot speak with managers, get no feedback and lack labour protections; REsPecTMe collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries and 98 expert interviews across care, gig and creative work in eight European countries to measure the unpaid labour buried inside paid work. Measurement and standard-setting: iLABOUR analysed how online labour markets pull workers out of national frameworks such as employment law and collective bargaining and impose their own technologically enforced institutions; GIGSTATS turned its Online Labour Index into a public statistics tool for work transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps; FAIRWORK co-develops fair work principles and rates and ranks platforms against them. Regulation and collective action: PLUS studies AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber across seven European cities to produce a Chart for digital workers' rights plus taxation and regulation guidelines, and COGONU maps every episode of food delivery couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016.

evidence:
Per gold project, the passages that satisfy "workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces".

**639652 iLABOUR** - report summary: "The 'gig economy' or 'platform economy' has emerged as a key theme in debates around digitalisation and the future of work. It can be defined as \"people using apps and websites, commonly known as platforms, to sell their labour\". The gig economy consists both of work that is transacted via platforms but delivered locally, and work that is transacted and delivered remotely over the Internet." Objective: "online labour markets that connect firms with knowledge and service workers around the world have grown up to 60% a year... An overlooked aspect of these markets is that they extricate workers and employers from national institutional frameworks, such as employment law and collective bargaining, and instead impose their own, technologically enforced institutions. For example, a leading marketplace recently instated a global minimum wage of 4.00 USD/h."

**759776 PLABOR** - report workPerformed: "So-called \"gig economy\" platforms in particular provide much needed income opportunities for people who have a distance to regular labor markets due to their legal status or gendered care duties at home. We have established that platform-based gig work is predominantly migrant work, given how relatively easy it is for (irregular) migrants to get started on a platform. Yet we also document how gig platforms introduce new risks and vuln[erabilities]". Objective: "determining how on-demand labor platforms distribute new opportunities and vulnerabilities for workers along gender, class, and racial lines... a cross-national comparative study that examines how platforms operate in three quickly growing and distinct tech hubs: Amsterdam, Berlin, and New York City."

**822638 PLUS** - report workPerformed: "a field work research on platform labour in terms of work organization, skills and social protections". Objective: "PLUS frames a ground-breaking grid of investigation that intertwines four disruptive platforms (AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber) and seven European cities (Barcelona, Berlin, Bologna, Lisbon, London, Paris, Tallinn)... in order to... produce outputs directly impacting on policy-making, market and welfare: innovative typologies of contracts, a Chart for digital workers' rights, taxation and regulation guidelines".

**833577 REsPecTMe** - report summary: "We collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, and 98 expert interviews across three work areas: creative, gig, and care work, in eight European countries." Report workPerformed: "we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries." Objective: "newly emerging on- and offline work in the gig economy for which people in paid work are not compensated or where it is used to access paid work."

**838081 FAIRWORK** - objective: "Millions of platform workers live all over the world: doing work that is outsourced via platforms or apps in the 'gig economy.' Workers tend to have little ability to negotiate wages or working conditions with the platforms that give them work... many workers have jobs characterized by long and irregular hours, low income, and high stress... It seeks to co-develop fair work principles with key stakeholders, develop methods to assess those principles, and ultimately rate and rank platforms against how they score against the fair work principles."

**875255 GIGSTATS** - objective: "existing economic statistics are not well suited to measuring work that is transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps (the so-called online gig economy). To address this problem, as part of the ERC-funded research project iLABOUR, we have developed the \"Online Labour Index\" (OLI), an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics. The OLI has already had major international social impact by exposing the geographic and occupational divisions in the otherwise invisible online labour market." Report teaser: "The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy, which refers to work transacted fully digitally via websites and apps. The gig economy constitutes a new and rapidly growing form of non-standard work, which is already the main source of income for approximately 1% of the..."

**101003134 GHOSTWORK** - objective: "This on-demand work is offered and performed online, paid by the task, on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. Conceptualized as 'ghost work', this rapidly growing, platform-based work is largely unseen: workers are unable to speak with managers, do not get feedback, and lack labour protections. How do these specific work conditions influence ghost workers' well-being?"

**101028811 COGONU** - objective: "In response to the rise of a new labour governance regime in the platform economy, militant forms of worker mobilization have recently emerged across Europe... it maps all episodes of couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016 accounting for similarities and differences in terms of strategies, action repertoire, and mobilization capacity." Report summary: "The rise of digital labour and the platform economy has triggered a burgeoning public interest in the topic of technological innovation in the workplace. However, only a few research projects have explored the conditions of workers."

Discrimination counter-examples, quoted, showing the boundary is in the text and not in a tag:

- **947806 iManage** (OUT) - "employment law has paid scant attention to the rise of algorithmic management: the increasingly pervasive reliance on monitoring technology and sophisticated algorithms to measure, control, and sanction workers... How can employment law respond to a world in which automation has not replaced workers - but their bosses?" The gig economy is named once as context; the study population is employees under algorithmic supervision, not people whose jobs arrive through an app.
- **893888 Boss Ex Machina** (OUT) - "cyber-physical devices make it possible to implement new practices of organizing, executing, monitoring and evaluating employees' performance - in each and every industry."
- **837539 Mercurius Connect** (OUT) - "Mercurius Connect platform, a Gig economy marketplace where RT Centres can find highly specialised dosimetrists, from all over the world, to perform clinical dosimetries on demand." It builds a marketplace; it studies no workers. Same reason retires 877557 WorkPilots ("a SaaS-based mobile-first on-demand job matching platform"), 837395 Gigstarter, 862780 TaxiDriver, 876581 SWIFTLY, 808366 TiMMi Transport, 674203 CAIN, 652511 CroDS.
- **890434 SOJUFOW** (OUT) - "develop and defend a theory of justice for contemporary labour markets in the light of recent and ongoing changes... (in particular the rise of automation, the changing nature of the firm, and the evolution of the gig economy)... I will explore these issues using the tools of normative political philosophy."
- **757395 WorkOD** (OUT) - its stated aim is "to develop a new methodology for the study of the key legal concept of the contract for work"; gig work enters only as "trends in the field including, in particular, the increased use of forms of contract... including those typical of task- or 'gig'-based work in the on-demand economy."
- **639403 WORKANDHOME** (OUT, ranked dense 13 / rerank 4) - "We went directly into neighbourhoods to identify home-based self-employed workers and used digital platforms to study home-based self-employment and freelancing in the digital economy": platforms are its data source; its subject is working from home.
- **101022491 ride-hailing** (OUT) - "the project will estimate how ride-hailing affects public transportation... To measure the effect of UBer on transit, I will estimate how the introduction of new subway stops affects Uber ridership." The unit of study is transit ridership, not drivers.

Sweep numbers, executed this session: the candidate's own probe (`objective/title ILIKE '%gig economy%'`) still returns exactly the six recorded ids; the title/objective term sweep returns 21 rows, of which 671524, 686782, 729930, 782009, 817010, 861598, 861833, 958171, 101003517, 101007770 are substring artifacts ("a digital platform working as a community of practice", "iadp platform work package 3.6", "an on-demand commerce platform"); the report-text sweep returns 43 rows and the second synonym wave returns 38 (title/objective) and 19 (report). euroSciVoc offers nothing usable: the only vocabulary titles matching gig/platform/precarious/labour/employment/sharing-economy are `employment` (787 projects) and `unemployment` (79).
why_good: This question discriminates on a boundary that lives only in free text: three different families of project use the same vocabulary - social-science studies of app-mediated work, legal studies of algorithmic management inside ordinary employment, and SMEs building gig marketplaces - and only the first satisfies the question. A system that keys on the phrase "gig economy" will pull in Mercurius Connect and iManage and miss GHOSTWORK and COGONU, which never use it in their titles. It fills the economics-and-business bucket at L3 with a labour topic distinct from vec-09's firm-network tax evasion, and adds a paraphrase-styled survey whose gold is spread across ERC, MSCA and RIA projects from 2015 to 2021. The L3 `survey` label is arithmetic: eight gold projects, each verified by reading its own objective or report text, so |gold| >= 5.

record.text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
record.reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in producing short chord sequences - up to eight chords - as a 'musical sketchpad' for electronic musicians, producers and DJs, aiming to inspire rather than to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered finished royalty-free soundtracks for movies, games and advertising at the touch of a button, moving from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API for third-party developers and validating willingness to pay through its 2019 public beta. CALMUSgaming, built by the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist on its CALMUS technology, delivered background music that is generated and re-adapted in real time as a computer game's plot and the player's actions evolve, claiming to save up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition. FlowMachines instead treated musical style itself as the sellable asset: its proof-of-concept built a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business, studied three business models in the movie, game and advertisement sectors, and worked to clear the legal issues around exploiting style.

record.text: Some EU projects build solar-fuel photoelectrodes out of carbon nitride rather than a metal-based semiconductor, so they have to work out how to make the material themselves. How do those projects differ in the routes they use to produce and deposit the carbon nitride layer?
record.reference_answer: MFreePEC works bottom-up from the molecule: it encodes the composition of a family of metal-free CNX materials (X = P, B or S) into supramolecular precursors, uses the stable intermediate melem to synthesise CN photoanodes in the 5-20 min range at higher temperatures, and gets the layer onto transparent conductive electrodes by electrophoretic deposition, ultrasonic spray of precursors, doctor-blading, dip-coating and added precursor vapour pressure during calcination - a porous carbon-nitride photoanode containing reduced graphene oxide and a nickel-iron oxyhydroxide oxidation co-catalyst held photocurrents exceeding 0.45 mA/cm2 at 1.23 V vs. NHE for more than 35 h. CALSOL instead pits two whole synthesis routes against each other for its carbon-based artificial leaf - the traditional thermal polycondensation route and a plasma polymerization route - and its headline result is negative about the traditional one: the product of thermal polycondensation of melamine is not graphitic carbon nitride but a defective melon structure that degraded considerably during photoelectrochemical experiments, with a flatband potential drifting from approx. -1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl to -1.8 vs. Ag/AgCl across pH. The contrast is therefore between engineering precursor chemistry and deposition method to build a durable working photoanode (MFreePEC) and testing whether an established preparation route yields a usable carbon nitride photoelectrode material at all (CALSOL).
record.notes: Seeds: 849068 MFreePEC and 797781 CALSOL, the only two projects whose text shows carbon nitride itself being made and deposited as the photoactive layer of a solar-fuel photoelectrode. record.text: Some EU projects build solar-fuel photoelectrodes out of carbon nitride rather than a metal-based semiconductor, so they have to work out how to make the material themselves. How do those projects differ in the routes they use to produce and deposit the carbon nitride layer?
record.reference_answer: MFreePEC works bottom-up from the molecule: it encodes the composition of a family of metal-free CNX materials (X = P, B or S) into supramolecular precursors, uses the stable intermediate melem to synthesise CN photoanodes in the 5-20 min range at higher temperatures, and gets the layer onto transparent conductive electrodes by electrophoretic deposition, ultrasonic spray of precursors, doctor-blading, dip-coating and added precursor vapour pressure during calcination - a porous carbon-nitride photoanode containing reduced graphene oxide and a nickel-iron oxyhydroxide oxidation co-catalyst held photocurrents exceeding 0.45 mA/cm2 at 1.23 V vs. NHE for more than 35 h. CALSOL instead pits two whole synthesis routes against each other for its carbon-based artificial leaf - the traditional thermal polycondensation route and a plasma polymerization route - and its headline result is negative about the traditional one: the product of thermal polycondensation of melamine is not graphitic carbon nitride but a defective melon structure that degraded considerably during photoelectrochemical experiments, with a flatband potential drifting from approx. -1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl to -1.8 vs. Ag/AgCl across pH. The contrast is therefore between engineering precursor chemistry and deposition method to build a durable working photoanode (MFreePEC) and testing whether an established preparation route yields a usable carbon nitride photoelectrode material at all (CALSOL).

record.text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
record.reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and concludes that multinationals dominate the political scene while sector associations decline in relative importance; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups on corporate tax cuts, payroll tax cuts and deregulation of employment protection in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States, and finds that government responsiveness depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a regulator's choice between an emission tax and an emission limit; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy, GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries, EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies between 1958 and 1992, EURECON studies the influence of commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making, and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.
record.notes: Seeds: PROSPER 842868 and LOBFRAM 657949 from the corpus-profile candidate (social sciences/political sciences bucket), read before the question existed; the question was composed from PROSPER's 'firms ... influence trade policymaking' and LOBFRAM's 'non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups'. Candidate drift check: the candidate's in-bucket lobbying cluster re-executes to 9 members (whole-word 'lobb' over objective inside 'social sciences/political sciences%'), not 5; the corpus-wide unfenced counts are 17 projects with 'lobb' in project.objective and 84 with 'lobb' in objective or any report_text section, so the euroSciVoc fence was dropped and the gold set was built corpus-wide. Gold rule applied mechanically: IN iff the project's own research, as stated in its objective or in its published report sections, examines efforts by companies, corporations or organised business interests to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making. OUT: the project's own advocacy or dissemination lobbying; passing background mentions; interest groups not identified as business. record.text: Which projects study the workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces, such as couriers, drivers, or people paid task by task over the internet?
record.reference_answer: Eight projects study this workforce, in three groups. Fieldwork on who these workers are and what the work does to them: PLABOR established that platform-based gig work in Amsterdam, Berlin and New York City is predominantly migrant work and documents the new risks it creates; GHOSTWORK follows the people who clean, code and classify data for AI on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, who cannot speak with managers, get no feedback and lack labour protections; REsPecTMe collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries and 98 expert interviews across care, gig and creative work in eight European countries to measure the unpaid labour buried inside paid work. Measurement and standard-setting: iLABOUR analysed how online labour markets pull workers out of national frameworks such as employment law and collective bargaining and impose their own technologically enforced institutions; GIGSTATS turned its Online Labour Index into a public statistics tool for work transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps; FAIRWORK co-develops fair work principles and rates and ranks platforms against them. Regulation and collective action: PLUS studies AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber across seven European cities to produce a Chart for digital workers' rights plus taxation and regulation guidelines, and COGONU maps every episode of food delivery couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016.

evidence:
Per gold project, the passages that satisfy "workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces".

**639652 iLABOUR** - report summary: "The 'gig economy' or 'platform economy' has emerged as a key theme in debates around digitalisation and the future of work. It can be defined as \"people using apps and websites, commonly known as platforms, to sell their labour\". The gig economy consists both of work that is transacted via platforms but delivered locally, and work that is transacted and delivered remotely over the Internet." Objective: "online labour markets that connect firms with knowledge and service workers around the world have grown up to 60% a year... An overlooked aspect of these markets is that they extricate workers and employers from national institutional frameworks, such as employment law and collective bargaining, and instead impose their own, technologically enforced institutions. For example, a leading marketplace recently instated a global minimum wage of 4.00 USD/h."

**759776 PLABOR** - report workPerformed: "So-called \"gig economy\" platforms in particular provide much needed income opportunities for people who have a distance to regular labor markets due to their legal status or gendered care duties at home. We have established that platform-based gig work is predominantly migrant work, given how relatively easy it is for (irregular) migrants to get started on a platform. Yet we also document how gig platforms introduce new risks and vuln[erabilities]". Objective: "determining how on-demand labor platforms distribute new opportunities and vulnerabilities for workers along gender, class, and racial lines... a cross-national comparative study that examines how platforms operate in three quickly growing and distinct tech hubs: Amsterdam, Berlin, and New York City."

**822638 PLUS** - report workPerformed: "a field work research on platform labour in terms of work organization, skills and social protections". Objective: "PLUS frames a ground-breaking grid of investigation that intertwines four disruptive platforms (AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber) and seven European cities (Barcelona, Berlin, Bologna, Lisbon, London, Paris, Tallinn)... in order to... produce outputs directly impacting on policy-making, market and welfare: innovative typologies of contracts, a Chart for digital workers' rights, taxation and regulation guidelines".

**833577 REsPecTMe** - report summary: "We collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, and 98 expert interviews across three work areas: creative, gig, and care work, in eight European countries." Report workPerformed: "we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries." Objective: "newly emerging on- and offline work in the gig economy for which people in paid work are not compensated or where it is used to access paid work."

**838081 FAIRWORK** - objective: "Millions of platform workers live all over the world: doing work that is outsourced via platforms or apps in the 'gig economy.' Workers tend to have little ability to negotiate wages or working conditions with the platforms that give them work... many workers have jobs characterized by long and irregular hours, low income, and high stress... It seeks to co-develop fair work principles with key stakeholders, develop methods to assess those principles, and ultimately rate and rank platforms against how they score against the fair work principles."

**875255 GIGSTATS** - objective: "existing economic statistics are not well suited to measuring work that is transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps (the so-called online gig economy). To address this problem, as part of the ERC-funded research project iLABOUR, we have developed the \"Online Labour Index\" (OLI), an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics. The OLI has already had major international social impact by exposing the geographic and occupational divisions in the otherwise invisible online labour market." record.text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
record.reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in producing short chord sequences - up to eight chords - as a 'musical sketchpad' for electronic musicians, producers and DJs, aiming to inspire rather than to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered finished royalty-free soundtracks for movies, games and advertising at the touch of a button, moving from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API for third-party developers and validating willingness to pay through its 2019 public beta. CALMUSgaming, built by the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist on its CALMUS technology, delivered background music that is generated and re-adapted in real time as a computer game's plot and the player's actions evolve, claiming to save up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition. FlowMachines instead treated musical style itself as the sellable asset: its proof-of-concept built a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business, studied three business models in the movie, game and advertisement sectors, and worked to clear the legal issues around exploiting style.

record.text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
record.reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in producing short chord sequences - up to eight chords - as a 'musical sketchpad' for electronic musicians, producers and DJs, aiming to inspire rather than to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered finished royalty-free soundtracks for movies, games and advertising at the touch of a button, moving from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API for third-party developers and validating willingness to pay through its 2019 public beta. CALMUSgaming, built by the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist on its CALMUS technology, delivered background music that is generated and re-adapted in real time as a computer game's plot and the player's actions evolve, claiming to save up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition. FlowMachines instead treated musical style itself as the sellable asset: its proof-of-concept built a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business, studied three business models in the movie, game and advertisement sectors, and worked to clear the legal issues around exploiting style.

record.text: Which projects study the workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces, such as couriers, drivers, or people paid task by task over the internet?
record.reference_answer: Eight projects study this workforce, in three groups. Fieldwork on who these workers are and what the work does to them: PLABOR established that platform-based gig work in Amsterdam, Berlin and New York City is predominantly migrant work and documents the new risks it creates; GHOSTWORK follows the people who clean, code and classify data for AI on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, who cannot speak with managers, get no feedback and lack labour protections; REsPecTMe collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries and 98 expert interviews across care, gig and creative work in eight European countries to measure the unpaid labour buried inside paid work. Measurement and standard-setting: iLABOUR analysed how online labour markets pull workers out of national frameworks such as employment law and collective bargaining and impose their own technologically enforced institutions; GIGSTATS turned its Online Labour Index into a public statistics tool for work transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps; FAIRWORK co-develops fair work principles and rates and ranks platforms against them. Regulation and collective action: PLUS studies AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber across seven European cities to produce a Chart for digital workers' rights plus taxation and regulation guidelines, and COGONU maps every episode of food delivery couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016.
record.notes: Seeds: candidate vector-43 supplied six ids from an ILIKE '%gig economy%' probe (833577, 837539, 838081, 875255, 890434, 947806); re-executed this session, still exactly those six. The probe was treated as a substring probe, not a gold set. GOLD (8): 639652 iLABOUR (online labour markets, their institutions and worker movements); 759776 PLABOR (on-demand labour platforms, migrant platform workers in Amsterdam/Berlin/NYC); 822638 PLUS (platform labour in seven cities, Deliveroo/Uber/Helpling/AirBnb); 833577 REsPecTMe (precariousness measured across care, gig and creative work, 414 biographical interviews); 838081 FAIRWORK (platform workers' pay and conditions, rating platforms); 875255 GIGSTATS (Online Labour Index measuring work transacted via websites and apps); 101003134 GHOSTWORK (Mechanical Turk microtask workers' well-being); 101028811 COGONU (food delivery couriers' mobilizations). DELIBERATE NEAR-MISSES, all read in full: 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina OUT - both study algorithmic monitoring and management of employees in conventional employment ('in each and every industry'), not workers whose jobs come through apps; 890434 SOJUFOW OUT - normative political philosophy of labour-market justice, gig economy named only as one of three trends, no study of the workers; 757395 WorkOD OUT - labour-law methodology for contracting for work, gig-based work an instance explained; 715950 SHARE OUT - solo self-employment generally; 822296 BEYOND4.0 OUT - Industry 4.0 impacts on work broadly; 895305 DweLinks OUT - short-term rental markets, not workers; 867466 YouthExistInTourism OUT - tourism employment in Goa and Lisbon, 'gig economies' used loosely, not app-mediated; 101022491 ride-hailing OUT - estimates ride-hailing's effect on public transport ridership, not on drivers; 639403 WORKANDHOME OUT - home-based self-employment and businesses, digital platforms only a data source. evidence:
Per gold project, the passages that satisfy "workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces".

**639652 iLABOUR** - report summary: "The 'gig economy' or 'platform economy' has emerged as a key theme in debates around digitalisation and the future of work. It can be defined as \"people using apps and websites, commonly known as platforms, to sell their labour\". The gig economy consists both of work that is transacted via platforms but delivered locally, and work that is transacted and delivered remotely over the Internet." Objective: "online labour markets that connect firms with knowledge and service workers around the world have grown up to 60% a year... An overlooked aspect of these markets is that they extricate workers and employers from national institutional frameworks, such as employment law and collective bargaining, and instead impose their own, technologically enforced institutions. For example, a leading marketplace recently instated a global minimum wage of 4.00 USD/h."

**759776 PLABOR** - report workPerformed: "So-called \"gig economy\" platforms in particular provide much needed income opportunities for people who have a distance to regular labor markets due to their legal status or gendered care duties at home. We have established that platform-based gig work is predominantly migrant work, given how relatively easy it is for (irregular) migrants to get started on a platform. Yet we also document how gig platforms introduce new risks and vuln[erabilities]". Objective: "determining how on-demand labor platforms distribute new opportunities and vulnerabilities for workers along gender, class, and racial lines... a cross-national comparative study that examines how platforms operate in three quickly growing and distinct tech hubs: Amsterdam, Berlin, and New York City."

**822638 PLUS** - report workPerformed: "a field work research on platform labour in terms of work organization, skills and social protections". Objective: "PLUS frames a ground-breaking grid of investigation that intertwines four disruptive platforms (AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber) and seven European cities (Barcelona, Berlin, Bologna, Lisbon, London, Paris, Tallinn)... in order to... produce outputs directly impacting on policy-making, market and welfare: innovative typologies of contracts, a Chart for digital workers' rights, taxation and regulation guidelines".

**833577 REsPecTMe** - report summary: "We collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, and 98 expert interviews across three work areas: creative, gig, and care work, in eight European countries." Report workPerformed: "we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries." Objective: "newly emerging on- and offline work in the gig economy for which people in paid work are not compensated or where it is used to access paid work."

**838081 FAIRWORK** - objective: "Millions of platform workers live all over the world: doing work that is outsourced via platforms or apps in the 'gig economy.' Workers tend to have little ability to negotiate wages or working conditions with the platforms that give them work... many workers have jobs characterized by long and irregular hours, low income, and high stress... It seeks to co-develop fair work principles with key stakeholders, develop methods to assess those principles, and ultimately rate and rank platforms against how they score against the fair work principles."

**875255 GIGSTATS** - objective: "existing economic statistics are not well suited to measuring work that is transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps (the so-called online gig economy). To address this problem, as part of the ERC-funded research project iLABOUR, we have developed the \"Online Labour Index\" (OLI), an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics. The OLI has already had major international social impact by exposing the geographic and occupational divisions in the otherwise invisible online labour market." record.text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
record.reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in for chord sequence generation, pitched to electronic musicians, producers and DJs as a 'musical sketchpad'; it deliberately stays small - predominantly sequences of up to eight chords - because its stated aim is to 'inspire' for composing, not to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered content creators finished royalty-free soundtracks 'in the matter of seconds, and at the touch of a button', transitioning from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API that lets third-party developers create hundreds of hours of soundtrack music, and it validated commercial feasibility by testing users' response and willingness to pay for the Music Engine public beta released in the second half of 2019. CALMUSgaming, from the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist and built on its CALMUS technology, targeted computer games instead: its report says the software generates new background music as the game evolves, with minimal contribution from the composer, saving up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition, and the funded work was a feasibility study covering technical scope, markets and competition, a patent search and a 5-year financial forecast. FlowMachines, a PoC of the ERC Flow-Machines project, treated musical style itself as the asset to sell and set out to build a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business - music composed to be synchronized to existing media such as advertisements, movie music or video games - but its report concludes that 'Direct commercial exploitation of AI technologies per se is no longer a profitable route', that the team shifted to producing, distributing and monetizing content by the music industry's 'traditional means', and that they convinced top executives of a major music label to create a dedicated label specialized in the production and dissemination of music composed with AI technologies; on the legal side it catalogued the copyright issues in a report but 'considered that it was not worth addressing the issues raised by each copyright type'.
