record.text: Which projects study the workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces, such as couriers, drivers, or people paid task by task over the internet?
record.reference_answer: Eight projects study this workforce, in three groups. Fieldwork on who these workers are and what the work does to them: PLABOR established that platform-based gig work in Amsterdam, Berlin and New York City is predominantly migrant work and documents the new risks it creates; GHOSTWORK follows the people who clean, code and classify data for AI on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, who cannot speak with managers, get no feedback and lack labour protections; REsPecTMe collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries and 98 expert interviews across care, gig and creative work in eight European countries to measure the unpaid labour buried inside paid work. Measurement and standard-setting: iLABOUR analysed how online labour markets pull workers out of national frameworks such as employment law and collective bargaining and impose their own technologically enforced institutions; GIGSTATS turned its Online Labour Index into a public statistics tool for work transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps and used it to measure that workforce itself - roughly 60% growth over five years, its geographic and occupational divisions, and women's participation in it; FAIRWORK co-develops fair work principles and rates and ranks platforms against them. Regulation and collective action: PLUS studies AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber across seven European cities to produce a Chart for digital workers' rights plus taxation and regulation guidelines, and COGONU maps every episode of food delivery couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016.
record.notes: Seeds: candidate vector-43 supplied six ids from an ILIKE '%gig economy%' probe (833577, 837539, 838081, 875255, 890434, 947806); re-executed this session, still exactly those six. The probe was treated as a substring probe, not a gold set. GOLD (8): 639652 iLABOUR (online labour markets, their institutions and worker movements); 759776 PLABOR (on-demand labour platforms, migrant platform workers in Amsterdam/Berlin/NYC); 822638 PLUS (platform labour in seven cities, Deliveroo/Uber/Helpling/AirBnb); 833577 REsPecTMe (precariousness measured across care, gig and creative work, 414 biographical interviews); 838081 FAIRWORK (platform workers' pay and conditions, rating platforms); 875255 GIGSTATS (Online Labour Index measuring work transacted via websites and apps); 101003134 GHOSTWORK (Mechanical Turk microtask workers' well-being); 101028811 COGONU (food delivery couriers' mobilizations). IN/OUT CRITERION (added at the fix round, settles 875255 against 101022491): a project is IN if the app-mediated workforce is itself the object being characterised - who these workers are, where they are, what they earn, what conditions they face - whether characterised one worker at a time or only in aggregate; it is OUT if those workers appear only as an input, a channel or context in a study whose object is something else. 875255 GIGSTATS is IN on the aggregate side: its report summary states 'The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy', 'we made significant advances in measuring the global online workforce', 'our OLI data revealed that the online gig economy grew approximately 60% over the past 5 years' and 'We expanded the topical and geographical scope of the OLI to Russian- and Spanish-language online freelance markets and to measuring the participation of women in the online gig economy' - the measured object is that workforce, even though no worker is interviewed and the objective text is proof-of-concept tooling (Excel-export interface, a public-organisation partnership, policy reports, a funding roadmap). 101022491 stays OUT under the same criterion: its two stated objectives are 'Estimate how ride-hailing affects public transit' and 'Discover the mechanisms by which public transit and ride-hailing affect each other', measured by estimating 'the effect of new subway stations on Uber ridership' - the measured object is transit ridership and the city, and drivers are never characterised at all. RE-CHECK OF THE EXCLUDED SET UNDER THIS CRITERION (re-read this round): 715950 SHARE is the closest call - it does measure a workforce in aggregate ('how the solo self-employed are classified, measured, and represented', labour-force surveys plus cross-national ethnography) and its summary says solo self-employment 'concerns both high- and low-skilled jobs, as well as those performed through digital labour platforms' - but its population is defined by contractual status, not by getting work through an app, and platform-performed work is one clause inside it with no platform-specific finding reported; stays OUT. 822296 BEYOND4.0 likewise names 'the digitisation of work through the platform economy (also referred to as Uberisation)' as one of its two transformations, but what it characterises is jobs, skills, tax and welfare systems, not the workers; OUT. 890434 SOJUFOW characterises nothing empirically (normative political philosophy); 757395 WorkOD's object is a methodology for the contract for work; 639403 WORKANDHOME's object is home-based self-employment; 867466 YouthExistInTourism's object is young people in touristified places; 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina study employees under algorithmic supervision in conventional employment ('in each and every industry'); 895305 DweLinks studies short-term rental markets - all unchanged and all OUT. Nothing else in the excluded set is pulled in by the criterion. 870619 WorkYP OUT (adjudicated at the fix round; it was never in the pool, and the ILIKE '%gig economy%' probe could not reach it because it writes the hyphenated form): its subject is in-work poverty across seven countries, and 'casual/zero-hours/gig-economy workers' is the fourth of four Vulnerable and Underrepresented Persons clusters, named in one clause of the objective and of the summary; its report's workPerformed and finalResults report only legal and policy outputs (EU social citizenship, 'fair and adequate wages', 29 deliverables, two conferences) and no finding about app-mediated workers. That standard reads consistently against 833577 REsPecTMe, which is IN not because gig work is listed among its sectors but because it fielded it: 'we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries', 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, 98 expert interviews. OTHER DELIBERATE NEAR-MISSES, all read in full: 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina OUT - both study algorithmic monitoring and management of employees in conventional employment, not workers whose jobs come through apps; 890434 SOJUFOW OUT - normative political philosophy of labour-market justice, gig economy named only as one of three trends, no study of the workers; 757395 WorkOD OUT - labour-law methodology for contracting for work, gig-based work an instance explained; 715950 SHARE OUT - solo self-employment generally; 822296 BEYOND4.0 OUT - Industry 4.0 impacts on work broadly; 895305 DweLinks OUT - short-term rental markets, not workers; 867466 YouthExistInTourism OUT - tourism employment in Goa and Lisbon, 'gig economies' used loosely, not app-mediated; 101022491 ride-hailing OUT - estimates ride-hailing's effect on public transport ridership, not on drivers; 639403 WORKANDHOME OUT - home-based self-employment and businesses, digital platforms only a data source. PLATFORM BUILDERS, all OUT (they create such marketplaces, they do not study the work): 837539 Mercurius Connect ('a Gig economy marketplace' for radiotherapy dosimetrists), 837395 C2C4LMB/Gigstarter, 877557 WorkPilots, 761756 Part-up, 862780 TaxiDriver, 876581 SWIFTLY, 808366 TiMMi Transport, 720657 DynaHUBS, 674203 CAIN, 652511 CroDS, 759207 P2PMODELS, 739349 P2Property, 775417 P2PCS. Other pooled candidates rejected on their best chunk as clearly off-topic: 880495 Citibox, 699017 TAG, 833105 Unispotter, 828151 Nello One, 101002867 CoDiM, 774802 BlockchainKYC, 763080 E-APIS, 651829 PILOTS, 722561 TEAM, 816538 MPA, 947307 HABIT, 833513 Lazzus, 947735 DATAFIED LIVING, 756672 HumanTrafficking, 830204 REACH, 770115 INCLUSION, 882828 RAYUELA, 658870 MigrWorkers, 768815 NSstop, 754506 CASEK, 735419 BizTweet, 808764 Talking Hands, 739832 IA-M-SHOP, 705366 MAStErS, 636427 SocialCar, 880895 UpSurgeOn Academy, 684116 Mobile E-Admini, 744719 Talkitt, 870702 HECAT, 873119 PRODIGEES. SWEEP (non-embedding, run at the drafting pass): over project.title||objective for gig econom/gig work/platform work/platform labo/labour|labor platform/crowdwork/crowd work/on-demand work/on-demand econom/app-based work/algorithmic management -> 21 hits, 9 of which were substring artifacts ('digital platform working as', 'platform work package', 'on-demand commerce platform'); over report_text (teaser+summary+workPerformed+finalResults) for the same terms -> 43 hits; second wave over both for ride-hailing/mechanical turk/microtask/click work/online freelanc/digital labour/online labour/ghost work/deliveroo/food delivery/Uber/Airbnb -> 38 + 19 hits. Every non-artifact hit was read and adjudicated. SWEEP EXTENSION (run at the fix round, over title||objective and over report title+teaser+summary+workPerformed+finalResults): LIKE '%gig-econom%' returns exactly 2 projects - 870619 WorkYP (adjudicated OUT above) and 761756 Part-up (already OUT, a platform builder); LIKE '%platform econom%' returns 14 - the gold 639652, 759776, 822638, 833577, 838081 and 101028811, the already-excluded 822296 BEYOND4.0 and 895305 DweLinks, and six projects not previously seen, all read this round and all clearly off-topic with the phrase as passing context: 678757 TRANSGENE (history of genome sequencing), 695256 BLINDSPOT (sociology of cognition in organizations), 760037 BIGlobal (firm growth and market power in trade), 854728 UNIFIED SCIENCE (an academic social-network product), 873112 Co-Change (RRI change labs), 957321 STADIEM (a media-startup accelerator). Neither form yields new gold. euroSciVoc has no leaf for this theme - the only related titles are 'employment' (787 projects) and 'unemployment' (79), far too coarse to enumerate, so the gold rests on the text sweep. TERM_STYLE paraphrase: the question uses none of the gold texts' distinctive vocabulary - no 'gig economy', 'platform work/labour', 'crowdwork', 'on-demand work', 'ghost work', 'algorithmic management', 'digital/online labour'; it says 'short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces'. evidence:
Per gold project, the passages that satisfy "workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces".

**639652 iLABOUR** - report summary: "The 'gig economy' or 'platform economy' has emerged as a key theme in debates around digitalisation and the future of work. It can be defined as \"people using apps and websites, commonly known as platforms, to sell their labour\". The gig economy consists both of work that is transacted via platforms but delivered locally, and work that is transacted and delivered remotely over the Internet." Objective: "online labour markets that connect firms with knowledge and service workers around the world have grown up to 60% a year... An overlooked aspect of these markets is that they extricate workers and employers from national institutional frameworks, such as employment law and collective bargaining, and instead impose their own, technologically enforced institutions. For example, a leading marketplace recently instated a global minimum wage of 4.00 USD/h."

**759776 PLABOR** - report workPerformed: "So-called \"gig economy\" platforms in particular provide much needed income opportunities for people who have a distance to regular labor markets due to their legal status or gendered care duties at home. We have established that platform-based gig work is predominantly migrant work, given how relatively easy it is for (irregular) migrants to get started on a platform. Yet we also document how gig platforms introduce new risks and vuln[erabilities]". Objective: "determining how on-demand labor platforms distribute new opportunities and vulnerabilities for workers along gender, class, and racial lines... a cross-national comparative study that examines how platforms operate in three quickly growing and distinct tech hubs: Amsterdam, Berlin, and New York City."

**822638 PLUS** - report workPerformed: "a field work research on platform labour in terms of work organization, skills and social protections". Objective: "PLUS frames a ground-breaking grid of investigation that intertwines four disruptive platforms (AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber) and seven European cities (Barcelona, Berlin, Bologna, Lisbon, London, Paris, Tallinn)... in order to... produce outputs directly impacting on policy-making, market and welfare: innovative typologies of contracts, a Chart for digital workers' rights, taxation and regulation guidelines".

**833577 REsPecTMe** - report summary: "We collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, and 98 expert interviews across three work areas: creative, gig, and care work, in eight European countries." Report workPerformed: "we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries." Objective: "newly emerging on- and offline work in the gig economy for which people in paid work are not compensated or where it is used to access paid work."

**838081 FAIRWORK** - objective: "Millions of platform workers live all over the world: doing work that is outsourced via platforms or apps in the 'gig economy.' Workers tend to have little ability to negotiate wages or working conditions with the platforms that give them work... many workers have jobs characterized by long and irregular hours, low income, and high stress... It seeks to co-develop fair work principles with key stakeholders, develop methods to assess those principles, and ultimately rate and rank platforms against how they score against the fair work principles."

**875255 GIGSTATS** - objective: "existing economic statistics are not well suited to measuring work that is transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps (the so-called online gig economy). To address this problem, as part of the ERC-funded research project iLABOUR, we have developed the \"Online Labour Index\" (OLI), an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics. The OLI has already had major international social impact by exposing the geographic and occupational divisions in the otherwise invisible online labour market." Report teaser: "The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy, which refers to work transacted fully digitally via websites and apps. The gig economy constitutes a new and rapidly growing form of non-standard work, which is already the main source of income for approximately 1% of the..."

**101003134 GHOSTWORK** - objective: "This on-demand work is offered and performed online, paid by the task, on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. Conceptualized as 'ghost work', this rapidly growing, platform-based work is largely unseen: workers are unable to speak with managers, do not get feedback, and lack labour protections. How do these specific work conditions influence ghost workers' well-being?"

**101028811 COGONU** - objective: "In response to the rise of a new labour governance regime in the platform economy, militant forms of worker mobilization have recently emerged across Europe... it maps all episodes of couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016 accounting for similarities and differences in terms of strategies, action repertoire, and mobilization capacity." Report summary: "The rise of digital labour and the platform economy has triggered a burgeoning public interest in the topic of technological innovation in the workplace. However, only a few research projects have explored the conditions of workers."

Discrimination counter-examples, quoted, showing the boundary is in the text and not in a tag:

- **947806 iManage** (OUT) - "employment law has paid scant attention to the rise of algorithmic management: the increasingly pervasive reliance on monitoring technology and sophisticated algorithms to measure, control, and sanction workers... How can employment law respond to a world in which automation has not replaced workers - but their bosses?" The gig economy is named once as context; the study population is employees under algorithmic supervision, not people whose jobs arrive through an app.
- **893888 Boss Ex Machina** (OUT) - "cyber-physical devices make it possible to implement new practices of organizing, executing, monitoring and evaluating employees' performance - in each and every industry."
- **837539 Mercurius Connect** (OUT) - "Mercurius Connect platform, a Gig economy marketplace where RT Centres can find highly specialised dosimetrists, from all over the world, to perform clinical dosimetries on demand." It builds a marketplace; it studies no workers. Same reason retires 877557 WorkPilots ("a SaaS-based mobile-first on-demand job matching platform"), 837395 Gigstarter, 862780 TaxiDriver, 876581 SWIFTLY, 808366 TiMMi Transport, 674203 CAIN, 652511 CroDS.
- **890434 SOJUFOW** (OUT) - "develop and defend a theory of justice for contemporary labour markets in the light of recent and ongoing changes... (in particular the rise of automation, the changing nature of the firm, and the evolution of the gig economy)... I will explore these issues using the tools of normative political philosophy."
- **757395 WorkOD** (OUT) - its stated aim is "to develop a new methodology for the study of the key legal concept of the contract for work"; gig work enters only as "trends in the field including, in particular, the increased use of forms of contract... including those typical of task- or 'gig'-based work in the on-demand economy."
- **639403 WORKANDHOME** (OUT, ranked dense 13 / rerank 4) - "We went directly into neighbourhoods to identify home-based self-employed workers and used digital platforms to study home-based self-employment and freelancing in the digital economy": platforms are its data source; its subject is working from home.
- **101022491 ride-hailing** (OUT) - "the project will estimate how ride-hailing affects public transportation... To measure the effect of UBer on transit, I will estimate how the introduction of new subway stops affects Uber ridership." The unit of study is transit ridership, not drivers.

Sweep numbers, executed this session: the candidate's own probe (`objective/title ILIKE '%gig economy%'`) still returns exactly the six recorded ids; the title/objective term sweep returns 21 rows, of which 671524, 686782, 729930, 782009, 817010, 861598, 861833, 958171, 101003517, 101007770 are substring artifacts ("a digital platform working as a community of practice", "iadp platform work package 3.6", "an on-demand commerce platform"); the report-text sweep returns 43 rows and the second synonym wave returns 38 (title/objective) and 19 (report). euroSciVoc offers nothing usable: the only vocabulary titles matching gig/platform/precarious/labour/employment/sharing-economy are `employment` (787 projects) and `unemployment` (79).
why_good: This question discriminates on a boundary that lives only in free text: three different families of project use the same vocabulary - social-science studies of app-mediated work, legal studies of algorithmic management inside ordinary employment, and SMEs building gig marketplaces - and only the first satisfies the question. A system that keys on the phrase "gig economy" will pull in Mercurius Connect and iManage and miss GHOSTWORK and COGONU, which never use it in their titles. It fills the economics-and-business bucket at L3 with a labour topic distinct from vec-09's firm-network tax evasion, and adds a paraphrase-styled survey whose gold is spread across ERC, MSCA and RIA projects from 2015 to 2021. The L3 `survey` label is arithmetic: eight gold projects, each verified by reading its own objective or report text, so |gold| >= 5.

findings.claim: Project 870619 WorkYP (Working, Yet Poor) studies gig-economy workers as one of its four named target populations across seven countries, and appears nowhere in the draft - not in gold_project_ids, not in the deliberate-near-miss list, not in the pooled-rejects list. It was never adjudicated at all, because the drafter's completeness rests on substring probes that structurally cannot see it.
findings.evidence: The drafter's swept terms include `gig econom`, which LIKE cannot match against the hyphenated form. Critic ran, over project.title||objective and over report_text (teaser+summary+workPerformed+finalResults): regexp_matches(lower(...), 'gig-econom|platform econom') -> 16 projects. Fifteen are already in gold, already documented OUT, or plainly off-topic. The sixteenth is 870619, matched on `gig-econom` only. Its report summary: "In each such Country, the WorkYP Project has identified four clusters of particularly Vulnerable and Underrepresented Persons (VUP Groups)... Such VUP Groups are: a) low wage workers; b) solo and bogus self-employed; c) flexible work contracts...; d) casual/zero-hours/gig-economy workers." Seven countries: Sweden, Italy, Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Poland. Critic's own MID rationale: WorkYP is marginal in the same direction the drafter already accepted for 833577 REsPecTMe; its workPerformed and finalResults report EU social-citizenship theory, deliverables and conferences, with no worker-level finding about app-mediated work. Defensible in and defensible out - but currently neither, and a system that returns it is scored wrong with no record of why. Level does not move: |gold| 8 -> 9, both L3.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - either add 870619 to gold_project_ids and pooling_evidence.accepted (level stays L3, survey), or add it to the notes' DELIBERATE NEAR-MISSES with the reason; the drafter's own "one clause naming the group, no worker-level study reported" reasoning would carry it. Separately the notes' sweep list would be more honest if the probes covered hyphenated and 'platform econom' forms, since the completeness argument rests on them.
findings.ruling_why: 870619 WorkYP names "casual/zero-hours/gig-economy workers" as one of four studied clusters and appears in neither gold, the near-miss list, nor the pooled rejects, and the critic showed why the drafter could not have seen it (the swept pattern `gig econom` cannot match the hyphenated form), so the completeness argument that carries this L3 survey has a hole exactly where its own probes were blind; the defect is that the project is un-adjudicated, not that it is certainly gold.

findings.claim: Gold member 875255 GIGSTATS does not study the workers; it is an ERC Proof-of-Concept grant to turn an existing index into a usable statistics product, and its unit of study is the aggregate online labour market. The drafter excluded 101022491 on exactly this ground.
findings.evidence: Full read of 875255. The objective's four stated work items are entirely tool work: "1) Develop a user-friendly online interface for the OLI that allows practitioners to export Excel files... 2) Establish a partnership with a public organization that will turn the OLI from a research experiment into a public tool... 3) Further disseminate the OLI's findings by writing policy reports... 4) Establish a roadmap and funding model for the future development and expansion of the OLI." The report summary's results are market aggregates - "our OLI data revealed that the online gig economy grew approximately 60% over the past 5 years", expansion to Russian- and Spanish-language markets, technology transfer to the ILO. No worker is interviewed, surveyed or observed. Compare the draft's own recorded exclusion of 101022491: "The unit of study is transit ridership, not drivers." Counterweight, why MID not HIGH: the summary does open "The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy", and one measured quantity is "the participation of women in the online gig economy", so a reading on which it studies the workforce in aggregate is defensible.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - two bounded options: drop 875255 from gold_project_ids and pooling_evidence.accepted (|gold| 7, still L3, and the reference answer's GIGSTATS sentence goes with it), or keep it and record in the notes why an aggregate-measurement project is IN while 101022491 is OUT, since the two currently sit on opposite sides of the same line with no stated distinction.
findings.ruling_why: The record puts 875255 GIGSTATS in gold while excluding 101022491 with the reason "the unit of study is transit ridership, not drivers", and GIGSTATS's own objective is four items of tool work over an aggregate market index with no worker studied, so the two sit on opposite sides of the same line with no stated distinction and an independent re-deriver cannot land on the recorded gold set; MID and not HIGH because the report summary does open on studying the online gig economy and measures women's participation in it, so an aggregate-workforce reading is defensible.

findings.claim: The draft's SEED-RETRIEVED note says 875255 GIGSTATS appears in no condition's top-20; true of the drafter's own pooling query but not of the theme generally.
findings.evidence: Critic reformulation "research on people who earn their income from short tasks posted on internet marketplaces, insecure piece-rate work without an employer" retrieved GIGSTATS at hybrid_rerank rank 2 and dense rank 10. Recorded because it cuts in the draft's favour: keeping GIGSTATS in gold is not asking systems to find something unfindable.

findings.claim: A courier/driver-led reformulation retrieved only COGONU from gold, filling all four conditions' top-20 with mobility and last-mile-logistics tech. The question's "such as couriers, drivers" clause pulls dense and lexical retrieval toward delivery technology rather than labour studies.
findings.evidence: Reformulation "couriers and drivers who get their jobs through a mobile phone application, paid per delivery or per ride" returned CriticalMaaS, Airmee, TiMMi, Citibox, SWIFTLY. Not a defect - the question is still answerable, as the second reformulation showed (5 of 8 gold) - but it is the shape of the discrimination this cell will measure.

judge_decisions.rationale: What this cell measures is a set-overlap score against an eight-project gold set on a boundary that exists only in free text, so the gold list is the instrument and both upheld findings land on it: one member is in on a criterion the record elsewhere uses to exclude, and one satisfying-or-not project was never adjudicated because the sweep that backs completeness was pattern-blind to it. Neither moves the level (7, 8 or 9 is L3 survey either way) and neither touches the question text, the paraphrase evidence or the recorded k=20 pooled run, so the fix is confined to gold membership and the notes - the cheapest class of change and one a cold drafter can execute from this record without re-verifying the question. The judge declined to let these ride as RECORDED because together they leave roughly one in eight of the scored gold contested and the record contradicting itself, which is the property "gold survives independent re-derivation" failing, and a bounded correction is available now that will not be available later. No stop rule fires.

evidence_carried_forward: evidence_carried_forward: the pooled retrieval (four conditions, k=20, 42 candidates, index fingerprint be84cbad9182), the rank matrix, the drafting-pass term sweeps (21/43 title-objective and 38/19 second-wave hits), the ILIKE '%gig economy%' seed probe, the euroSciVoc coverage check, and the per-gold passage reads for the seven gold projects other than 875255 were NOT re-run - the judge froze the question text and the recorded run, and neither edit changed the question, the pool, or the gold set, so no retrieval measurement was invalidated. 947806 iManage, 893888 Boss Ex Machina, 895305 DweLinks and the platform-builder list were also not re-read; their exclusion axis is untouched by the new criterion, so the drafter reasoned from the quotes already in the record rather than re-pulling the text. All of that is carried forward from the original pass and should be re-measured rather than trusted.

record.text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
record.reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and concludes that multinationals dominate the political scene while sector associations decline in relative importance; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups on corporate tax cuts, payroll tax cuts and deregulation of employment protection in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States, and finds that government responsiveness depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a regulator's choice between an emission tax and an emission limit; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy, GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries, EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies between 1958 and 1992, EURECON studies the influence of commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making, and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.

Question: "Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?"

Gold, with the passage that satisfies the question (passages drawn from a lowercasing SQL extract are marked [lc]):

1. **842868 PROSPER** - "Politics of Rulemaking, Orchestration of Standards, and Private Economic Regulations". Objective: "PROSPER will primarily investigate the extent to which MNCs are able to orchestrate political mobilization of their subsidiaries for coordinated lobbying and impose rules and standards upon firms along their supply chains." Report summary: "examine the role of private international actors, i.e., firms, which mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union (EU)." Report finalResults: "since particularly resourceful firms are able to carry their political demands to policymakers, interest representation might be skewed in their favor."
2. **840978 BIZPOL** - "Business as political actor". Objective: "CPA comprises all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests." Report summary/teaser: "as the best resourced and often most effective lobby force business also play a very important and consequential role in politics" [lc]. Report workPerformed: "An eco-system perspective was applied to map interest, influencing strategies and expectations of different relevant stakeholder groups".
3. **834253 TRASC** - "Trade Agreements and Supply Chains". Objective: "I will examine how large corporations with international supply chains shape the content and political support for deep RTAs". Report workPerformed: "We also study how firm-level lobbying shapes the content of FTAs. The dataset provides information on firms' lobbying effort to influence deep trade policies (e.g., intellectual property rights, investment rules, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, labor and environmental regulations)". Report summary: "i examine how lobbying by large corporations affects rtas (the probability that they are ratified, as well as the provisions included in them) and ad duties" [lc].
4. **705677 BUSWEL** - "Why is Business in Some Countries More Hostile to Social Redistribution than in Others?". Objective: "BUSWEL analyzes how the strategies and activities of business interest groups have contributed to these diverging outcomes. The project compares policy positions and strategies of business interest groups in five countries: Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria, and the United States." Report finalResults: "the focus of the project on government responsiveness toward business demands for tax cuts has moved our understanding of the impact of business interest groups on the politics of social inequality forward" [lc].
5. **748066 MILO** - "Mining, lobbying and efficient environmental policy". Objective: "investigate the optimal environmental policy of the mining sector with a special emphasis on ... the choice of policy instruments under lobbying ... new insights on the formation of lobby groups and policy instruments". Report summary: "the polluters can influence the policy maker's instrument choice ... by focusing on the firms' incentives to join the lobby group and by investigating the consequences of this to instrument choice" [lc]. Report finalResults: "extends the current literature on environmental policy and lobbying by letting the firms decide whether it is beneficial for them to be part of the lobby group" [lc].
6. **819394 DIA** - "Deep Integration Agreements" (report-only member; the objective never mentions lobbying). Report summary: "second, on regulatory cooperation, we examined how industry lobbying influences international rule-making, and showed that the impact on society depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests" [lc]. Report workPerformed: "organized around three pillars - investor protection, regulatory cooperation, and intellectual property rights - supplemented by related projects on industrial policy, lobbying, labor markets, and political distortions" [lc].
7. **658375 EFTA DEVELOPMENT** - "The 'other' Europe: the formation and development of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), 1958-92". Report summary: "assess how all relevant actors - national governments/efta officials and institutions/non-state actors like national trade union centres and business lobby groups - shaped the association's policies and priorities" [lc]. Report workPerformed: archives include "four different national trade union centres/business lobbies" [lc].
8. **657949 LOBFRAM** - "Lobbying and framing in foreign policy". Objective: "this project will explore the activities of non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups, NGOs and solidarity movements, in EU foreign policy, investigating the networks that are established at different levels (EU and member states) and framing processes." Report teaser: "The project aimed to advance our understanding of lobbying and framing in foreign policy in the European Union's (EU) system of multi-level governance."
9. **786587 IFDG** - "Innovation, firm dynamics and growth" (delivered strand). Report workPerformed: "the project on the impact of foreign competition on firms lobbying behavior has first consisted in collecting the datasets on lobbying expenditures, firms' financial information, patents and trade flows from different sources" [lc]. Report summary: "a fourth study looks at the extent to which us firms react more to increased competition from china by lobbying more" [lc]. Report finalResults: "we are also the first to focus on the indirect effect a shock in foreign competition can trigger in firms' lobbying expenses" [lc].
10. **798769 MIGPSC** - report summary states the research question: "how do private security actors and defence industry shape the european migration management policy inside and outside the eu borders?" [lc]; a second report passage: "rly true internally, at the policy-making level (essentially through lobbying), and externally, in particular in the mediterranean region" [lc].
11. **716849 EURECON** - "The Making of a Lopsided Union". Objective: "The project also intends to encourage the study of the critical influence of non-EEC and non-state actors and factors on the European decision-making level. To this end, the PI will lead a team ... to explore specific case studies involving commercial banks, big business, trade unions". Report: "komornicka showed the stable support but scant initiative of european business associations on emu" [lc].
12. **101024225 ClimActiv** - "Climate Activism and Harm to Innocents". Report summary: "the research focused on two forms of activism: climate direct action, and corporate climate lobbying" [lc]. Report finalResults: "the project developed a novel view on corporate lobbying's democratic credentials, and showed that corporate lobbying in favour of ambitious climate policies can be justified despite being undemocratic in important senses" [lc].
13. **714905 CITIZINGLOBAL** - "Citizens, Institutions and Globalization". Objective: "Part A studies the puzzling popularity of protectionism and how lobbies can raise it by manipulating information ... It will show that lobbies can raise protection by channeling information to insiders and advertising the plight of displaced workers." Report summary: "The project shows that powerful special interests can capture government decisions when citizens are poorly informed. Harmful consequences include inefficient protectionism, misallocation of public investment, unchecked pollution and insecurity of property rights."
14. **948516 PARTICIPATE** - report finalResults: "the working paper entitled 'tax incentives or political motivations? evidence from corporate contribution' ... provides the first estimation of the tax price elasticity of corporate giving using an exhaustive administrative panel dataset of firms ... we also contribute to the recent literature on 'tax-exempt lobbying' that shows that, at least in the u.s. context, corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics" [lc].
15. **741538 UneqDems** - "Unequal Democracies". Report: "ems explores the impact of austerity on policy-making processes and policy outputs in the netherlands, the other project focusing on the exercise of 'business power' in switzerland. both phd projects combine quantitative analyses ... with qualitative process-tracing" [lc].
16. **950056 GRIP-ARM** - "Green Industrial Policy in the Age of Rare Metals". Objective, research question 1: "How do state capacity, business power and organizational structure of domestic markets shape the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries?" Project status SIGNED (ongoing); its interim report covers "how industrial policy designs in both mineral producers and consumers have evolved" [lc] without repeating the business-power phrase.

findings.claim: POWERSHIFTS 751843 (Shifting political power: the nature and consequences of distributed renewable energy transitions) studies exactly what the question asks - how energy firms and industry groups exercise influence over energy policy - and it appears in neither gold_project_ids nor the 38 pooled rejections nor the named near-miss list, so it was never adjudicated.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([751843]). Report teaser/summary open with "Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits" and "Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes". The objective's research questions are to examine the conditions leading to shifts in political power, assess the mechanisms, and identify the consequences, with influence channels named as "changes in access to policy makers, media influence" and outcomes as "contested carbon targets, renewable energy subsidies". workPerformed: "RECs are increasingly adept at building political coalitions to increase their policy impact. This is most often with renewables companies and industry groups". That meets the drafter's own IN rule and is not the project's own advocacy nor a background mention. It reached dense rank 8 / hybrid 12 / hybrid_rerank 15 on the critic's reformulation, so a system under test can retrieve it and would be scored wrong for doing so. Why the sweeps could not find it, executed: regexp over objective+all report sections for 751843 returned no 'lobb' token anywhere (so S1 and S2 were structurally blind to it) and no match on the actor-first proximity order, only on the reverse policy-first order. The blind spot is directional and applies corpus-wide, so this is a mechanism, not a single slip: further members may be reachable only by opposed/resisted/pushed-for verbs and policy-first phrasing.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - adding 751843 makes gold 18 and leaves the cell at L3, so level and subtype are untouched; the reference answer would need one clause for it. The more durable edit is to re-run the completeness sweep with the proximity pattern in BOTH orders and with an opposition/advocacy verb set (oppose, resist, block, push for, campaign, advocate, press) before the gold is fixed, since the same gap that hid this project is still open.

findings.claim: PARTICIPATE 948516 is a campaign-finance and charitable-giving project; nothing it researches examines companies trying to influence the policies or regulations governments adopt, and the one sentence the draft relies on describes a literature the project contributes to, not its own finding.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([948516]), full summary/workPerformed/finalResults. The stated goal is "the study of campaign finance, information and influence" through the motives behind small campaign contributions, the tax-price elasticity of political donations, political selection and media exposure. The six workPerformed items are Small Campaign Donors, Is Charitable Giving Political?, The Far-Right Donation Gap, a Political Inequality review, a tax-treatment survey experiment, and Tax Incentives or Political Motivations? record.text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
record.reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and concludes that multinationals dominate the political scene while sector associations decline in relative importance; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups on corporate tax cuts, payroll tax cuts and deregulation of employment protection in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States, and finds that government responsiveness depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a regulator's choice between an emission tax and an emission limit; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy, GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries, EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies between 1958 and 1992, EURECON studies the influence of commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making, and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.
record.notes: Seeds: PROSPER 842868 and LOBFRAM 657949 from the corpus-profile candidate (social sciences/political sciences bucket), read before the question existed; the question was composed from PROSPER's 'firms ... influence trade policymaking' and LOBFRAM's 'non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups'. Candidate drift check: the candidate's in-bucket lobbying cluster re-executes to 9 members (whole-word 'lobb' over objective inside 'social sciences/political sciences%'), not 5; the corpus-wide unfenced counts are 17 projects with 'lobb' in project.objective and 84 with 'lobb' in objective or any report_text section, so the euroSciVoc fence was dropped and the gold set was built corpus-wide. Gold rule applied mechanically: IN iff the project's own research, as stated in its objective or in its published report sections, examines efforts by companies, corporations or organised business interests to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making. OUT: the project's own advocacy or dissemination lobbying; passing background mentions; interest groups not identified as business. Rejected pooled candidates (43 pooled, 38 rejected) include CONSULTATIONEFFECTS 804288 (studies consultation designs with 'citizens and interest organizations' generally, not business influence efforts), EUTIP 721916 (lobbyists appear only as network partner organisations), TiGRE 870722 / REGTRUST 101026008 (trust in regulation), IIT 649351, MABIS 101004099, OCIAN 789013, BHR_EU 843115 and the remaining pooled projects whose best chunk is off-topic. NEAR influenc/lobb/polic/legislat)' over objective+report for all not-yet-adjudicated projects - 7 rows, all read. S2/S3/S4 are what produced 12 of the 17 gold members; only 5 (PROSPER, TRASC, BIZPOL, BUSWEL, LOBFRAM) appeared in the pooled top-20. Named near-misses left OUT with reasons: REVEAL 725798 (stated research question is the resilience of private rule-making bodies, not efforts to shape government policy), TRADEPOWER 724107 (bargaining power of countries in trade negotiations; lobbying appears only in a link to legislators' district attitudes), POLBUSNETWORKS 724501 (firm-politician favour networks and misallocation, not policy or regulation), CLIFF 101020082 ('fossil fuel vested interests are lobbying heavily' is scene-setting in the summary), Digital Good 804985 (one workPerformed bullet listing tech-company lobbying on the European Health Data Space), IMPACT HAU 772544 (lobbyists named among ethnographic case sites), FEDCIT 740447 and PEMP 637662 (candidate sample_ids: FEDCIT's 'local actors' active lobbying' is by municipalities, and PEMP names lobbying only as a future application of its election model), DemocInChange 702134 (civil society organisations, not business), DEMSEC 639021 and CONSULTATIONEFFECTS 804288 (interest groups not identified as business). term_style paraphrase: 12 of the 17 gold texts use lobby/lobbying/lobbyist as their key term and the question uses none of that vocabulary, saying 'try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt' instead; consistent with the rank matrix, where only BUSWEL (lexical 8), PROSPER (lexical 13) and LOBFRAM (lexical 17) reach the lexical top-20 and the rest of the pooled gold is found by dense/hybrid/rerank. findings.claim: POWERSHIFTS 751843 (Shifting political power: the nature and consequences of distributed renewable energy transitions) studies exactly what the question asks - how energy firms and industry groups exercise influence over energy policy - and it appears in neither gold_project_ids nor the 38 pooled rejections nor the named near-miss list, so it was never adjudicated.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([751843]). Report teaser/summary open with "Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits" and "Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes". The objective's research questions are to examine the conditions leading to shifts in political power, assess the mechanisms, and identify the consequences, with influence channels named as "changes in access to policy makers, media influence" and outcomes as "contested carbon targets, renewable energy subsidies". workPerformed: "RECs are increasingly adept at building political coalitions to increase their policy impact. This is most often with renewables companies and industry groups". That meets the drafter's own IN rule and is not the project's own advocacy nor a background mention. It reached dense rank 8 / hybrid 12 / hybrid_rerank 15 on the critic's reformulation, so a system under test can retrieve it and would be scored wrong for doing so. Why the sweeps could not find it, executed: regexp over objective+all report sections for 751843 returned no 'lobb' token anywhere (so S1 and S2 were structurally blind to it) and no match on the actor-first proximity order, only on the reverse policy-first order. The blind spot is directional and applies corpus-wide, so this is a mechanism, not a single slip: further members may be reachable only by opposed/resisted/pushed-for verbs and policy-first phrasing.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - adding 751843 makes gold 18 and leaves the cell at L3, so level and subtype are untouched; the reference answer would need one clause for it. The more durable edit is to re-run the completeness sweep with the proximity pattern in BOTH orders and with an opposition/advocacy verb set (oppose, resist, block, push for, campaign, advocate, press) before the gold is fixed, since the same gap that hid this project is still open.
findings.ruling_why: The critic read 751843 POWERSHIFTS in full and showed it satisfies the drafter's own stated IN rule ("Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes", "RECs ... building political coalitions ... with renewables companies and industry groups"), it appears nowhere in gold, the 38 pooled rejections or the near-miss list, and it retrieves at dense 8 / hybrid 12 / rerank 15 - so a system that finds it is scored wrong; the drafter's four sweeps could not refute this because all of them were keyed on the `lobb` stem or on actor-first word order, which 751843 matches in neither.

findings.claim: PARTICIPATE 948516 is a campaign-finance and charitable-giving project; nothing it researches examines companies trying to influence the policies or regulations governments adopt, and the one sentence the draft relies on describes a literature the project contributes to, not its own finding.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([948516]), full summary/workPerformed/finalResults. The stated goal is "the study of campaign finance, information and influence" through the motives behind small campaign contributions, the tax-price elasticity of political donations, political selection and media exposure. The six workPerformed items are Small Campaign Donors, Is Charitable Giving Political?, The Far-Right Donation Gap, a Political Inequality review, a tax-treatment survey experiment, and Tax Incentives or Political Motivations? Evidence from Corporate Contribution, which estimates the tax price elasticity of corporate donations. The draft's supporting quote reads in full: "the working paper ... contributes to the literature by providing the first estimation of the tax price elasticity of corporate giving ... Furthermore, we also contribute to the recent literature on 'tax-exempt lobbying' that shows that, at least in the U.S. context, corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics." The influence claim belongs to the cited literature, and it is "influence politics", not policies or regulations governments adopt. This is the same weight of support the drafter itself rejected for CLIFF 101020082 and PEMP 637662.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - dropping 948516 leaves gold at 16 and the cell at L3, and removes one sentence from the reference answer. If kept, the record should say which of its own findings - not which cited literature - examines business influence on policy.
findings.ruling_why: On PARTICIPATE 948516 the critic quoted the drafter's own supporting sentence in full and it attributes the influence claim to a literature the project contributes to ("we also contribute to the recent literature on 'tax-exempt lobbying' that shows ..."), not to the project's own research, which is the same weight of support the drafter itself ruled insufficient for CLIFF 101020082 and PEMP 637662.

findings.claim: The membership rule is applied in two directions at once. CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 is IN although its influencers are never identified as business, while CONSERVATION 683031 was put OUT for exactly "lobbyists unspecified", and SPIKE 797989 - which turns up in the same 17-row S1 sweep and is in the same category - is adjudicated nowhere in the package.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([714905]): the objective says "how lobbies can raise [protectionism] by manipulating information ... lobbies can raise protection by channeling information to insiders"; the report summary says "powerful special interests can capture government decisions when citizens are poorly informed". Neither business, firm, corporate nor industry appears as the influencing actor anywhere in its text - the drafter discloses this itself. The draft's stated OUT rule is "interest groups not identified as business", applied to CONSERVATION 683031, DEMSEC 639021 and CONSULTATIONEFFECTS 804288. The critic re-ran S1 independently: regexp_matches(lower(objective),'\blobb') returns exactly 17 rows, reproducing the drafter's count. Four are gold (657949, 714905, 748066, 842868), four are named rejections (637662, 702134, 721916, 740447), nine are unmentioned. Eight of those nine are clean excludes under the stated rule (uP_running 691748, AB-Prevention 717273, IFASA 744848, SWEETENED HEARTS 898829 are the project's own advocacy; EuroAgeism 764632 trains lobbyists; N-T-AUTONOMY 758015 and TGL 845118 are minority groups and NGOs; INTERMESTIC 659369 is parliaments and unspecified interest groups). I will quantify the importance of lobbyist-client relationships", aiming to "inform the policy debate on how to reduce political corruption and improve the quality of regulation in advocacy services", and its workPerformed reports a unique dataset on lobbying efforts. Its influencers are unspecified lobbyists - the CITIZINGLOBAL situation exactly. So one of the two treatments is wrong; the record cannot support both.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY, and either direction keeps the cell at L3 - tighten the rule to "the influencing actor is identified as business in the project's own text" and drop 714905 (gold 16), or widen it to organised private interests and adjudicate 797989 and 683031 on the record. record.text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
record.reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in for chord sequence generation, pitched to electronic musicians, producers and DJs as a 'musical sketchpad'; it deliberately stays small - predominantly sequences of up to eight chords - because its stated aim is to 'inspire' for composing, not to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered content creators finished royalty-free soundtracks 'in the matter of seconds, and at the touch of a button', transitioning from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API that lets third-party developers create hundreds of hours of soundtrack music, and it validated commercial feasibility by testing users' response and willingness to pay for the Music Engine public beta released in the second half of 2019. CALMUSgaming, from the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist and built on its CALMUS technology, targeted computer games instead: its report says the software generates new background music as the game evolves, with minimal contribution from the composer, saving up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition, and the funded work was a feasibility study covering technical scope, markets and competition, a patent search and a 5-year financial forecast. FlowMachines, a PoC of the ERC Flow-Machines project, treated musical style itself as the asset to sell and set out to build a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business - music composed to be synchronized to existing media such as advertisements, movie music or video games - but its report concludes that 'Direct commercial exploitation of AI technologies per se is no longer a profitable route', that the team shifted to producing, distributing and monetizing content by the music industry's 'traditional means', and that they convinced top executives of a major music label to create a dedicated label specialized in the production and dissemination of music composed with AI technologies; on the legal side it catalogued the copyright issues in a report but 'considered that it was not worth addressing the issues raised by each copyright type'.
record.notes: Seed provenance: corpus-profile candidate vector-07 (euroSciVoc leaf 'computational creativity', 3 members - 659434 MUSICAL-MOODS, 754401 I2C8, 951908 eTryOn; re-executed this pass, still 3). record.text: Which projects study the workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces, such as couriers, drivers, or people paid task by task over the internet?
record.reference_answer: Eight projects study this workforce, in three groups. Fieldwork on who these workers are and what the work does to them: PLABOR established that platform-based gig work in Amsterdam, Berlin and New York City is predominantly migrant work and documents the new risks it creates; GHOSTWORK follows the people who clean, code and classify data for AI on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, who cannot speak with managers, get no feedback and lack labour protections; REsPecTMe collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries and 98 expert interviews across care, gig and creative work in eight European countries to measure the unpaid labour buried inside paid work. Measurement and standard-setting: iLABOUR analysed how online labour markets pull workers out of national frameworks such as employment law and collective bargaining and impose their own technologically enforced institutions; GIGSTATS turned its Online Labour Index into a public statistics tool for work transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps and used it to measure that workforce itself - roughly 60% growth over five years, its geographic and occupational divisions, and women's participation in it; FAIRWORK co-develops fair work principles and rates and ranks platforms against them. Regulation and collective action: PLUS studies AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber across seven European cities to produce a Chart for digital workers' rights plus taxation and regulation guidelines, and COGONU maps every episode of food delivery couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016.

IN/OUT CRITERION (added at the fix round, settles 875255 against 101022491): a project is IN if the app-mediated workforce is itself the object being characterised - who these workers are, where they are, what they earn, what conditions they face - whether characterised one worker at a time or only in aggregate; it is OUT if those workers appear only as an input, a channel or context in a study whose object is something else. 875255 GIGSTATS is IN on the aggregate side: its report summary states 'The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy', 'we made significant advances in measuring the global online workforce', 'our OLI data revealed that the online gig economy grew approximately 60% over the past 5 years' and 'We expanded the topical and geographical scope of the OLI to Russian- and Spanish-language online freelance markets and to measuring the participation of women in the online gig economy' - the measured object is that workforce, even though no worker is interviewed and the objective text is proof-of-concept tooling (Excel-export interface, a public-organisation partnership, policy reports, a funding roadmap). 101022491 stays OUT under the same criterion: its two stated objectives are 'Estimate how ride-hailing affects public transit' and 'Discover the mechanisms by which public transit and ride-hailing affect each other', measured by estimating 'the effect of new subway stations on Uber ridership' - the measured object is transit ridership and the city, and drivers are never characterised at all. RE-CHECK OF THE EXCLUDED SET UNDER THIS CRITERION (re-read this round): 715950 SHARE is the closest call - it does measure a workforce in aggregate ('how the solo self-employed are classified, measured, and represented', labour-force surveys plus cross-national ethnography) and its summary says solo self-employment 'concerns both high- and low-skilled jobs, as well as those performed through digital labour platforms' - but its population is defined by contractual status, not by getting work through an app, and platform-performed work is one clause inside it with no platform-specific finding reported; stays OUT. 822296 BEYOND4.0 likewise names 'the digitisation of work through the platform economy (also referred to as Uberisation)' as one of its two transformations, but what it characterises is jobs, skills, tax and welfare systems, not the workers; OUT. 890434 SOJUFOW characterises nothing empirically (normative political philosophy); 757395 WorkOD's object is a methodology for the contract for work; 639403 WORKANDHOME's object is home-based self-employment; 867466 YouthExistInTourism's object is young people in touristified places; 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina study employees under algorithmic supervision in conventional employment ('in each and every industry'); 895305 DweLinks studies short-term rental markets - all unchanged and all OUT. Nothing else in the excluded set is pulled in by the criterion. 870619 WorkYP OUT (adjudicated at the fix round; it was never in the pool, and the ILIKE '%gig economy%' probe could not reach it because it writes the hyphenated form): its subject is in-work poverty across seven countries, and 'casual/zero-hours/gig-economy workers' is the fourth of four Vulnerable and Underrepresented Persons clusters, named in one clause of the objective and of the summary; its report's workPerformed and finalResults report only legal and policy outputs (EU social citizenship, 'fair and adequate wages', 29 deliverables, two conferences) and no finding about app-mediated workers. That standard reads consistently against 833577 REsPecTMe, which is IN not because gig work is listed among its sectors but because it fielded it: 'we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries', 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, 98 expert interviews. OTHER DELIBERATE NEAR-MISSES, all read in full: 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina OUT - both study algorithmic monitoring and management of employees in conventional employment, not workers whose jobs come through apps; 890434 SOJUFOW OUT - normative political philosophy of labour-market justice, gig economy named only as one of three trends, no study of the workers; 757395 WorkOD OUT - labour-law methodology for contracting for work, gig-based work an instance explained; 715950 SHARE OUT - solo self-employment generally; 822296 BEYOND4.0 OUT - Industry 4.0 impacts on work broadly; 895305 DweLinks OUT - short-term rental markets, not workers; 867466 YouthExistInTourism OUT - tourism employment in Goa and Lisbon, 'gig economies' used loosely, not app-mediated; 101022491 ride-hailing OUT - estimates ride-hailing's effect on public transport ridership, not on drivers; 639403 WORKANDHOME OUT - home-based self-employment and businesses, digital platforms only a data source. evidence:
Per gold project, the passages that satisfy "workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces".

**639652 iLABOUR** - report summary: "The 'gig economy' or 'platform economy' has emerged as a key theme in debates around digitalisation and the future of work. It can be defined as \"people using apps and websites, commonly known as platforms, to sell their labour\". The gig economy consists both of work that is transacted via platforms but delivered locally, and work that is transacted and delivered remotely over the Internet." Objective: "online labour markets that connect firms with knowledge and service workers around the world have grown up to 60% a year... An overlooked aspect of these markets is that they extricate workers and employers from national institutional frameworks, such as employment law and collective bargaining, and instead impose their own, technologically enforced institutions. For example, a leading marketplace recently instated a global minimum wage of 4.00 USD/h."

**759776 PLABOR** - report workPerformed: "So-called \"gig economy\" platforms in particular provide much needed income opportunities for people who have a distance to regular labor markets due to their legal status or gendered care duties at home. We have established that platform-based gig work is predominantly migrant work, given how relatively easy it is for (irregular) migrants to get started on a platform. Yet we also document how gig platforms introduce new risks and vuln[erabilities]". Objective: "determining how on-demand labor platforms distribute new opportunities and vulnerabilities for workers along gender, class, and racial lines... a cross-national comparative study that examines how platforms operate in three quickly growing and distinct tech hubs: Amsterdam, Berlin, and New York City."

**822638 PLUS** - report workPerformed: "a field work research on platform labour in terms of work organization, skills and social protections". Objective: "PLUS frames a ground-breaking grid of investigation that intertwines four disruptive platforms (AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber) and seven European cities (Barcelona, Berlin, Bologna, Lisbon, London, Paris, Tallinn)... in order to... produce outputs directly impacting on policy-making, market and welfare: innovative typologies of contracts, a Chart for digital workers' rights, taxation and regulation guidelines".

**833577 REsPecTMe** - report summary: "We collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, and 98 expert interviews across three work areas: creative, gig, and care work, in eight European countries." Report workPerformed: "we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries." Objective: "newly emerging on- and offline work in the gig economy for which people in paid work are not compensated or where it is used to access paid work."

**838081 FAIRWORK** - objective: "Millions of platform workers live all over the world: doing work that is outsourced via platforms or apps in the 'gig economy.' Workers tend to have little ability to negotiate wages or working conditions with the platforms that give them work... many workers have jobs characterized by long and irregular hours, low income, and high stress... It seeks to co-develop fair work principles with key stakeholders, develop methods to assess those principles, and ultimately rate and rank platforms against how they score against the fair work principles."

**875255 GIGSTATS** - objective: "existing economic statistics are not well suited to measuring work that is transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps (the so-called online gig economy). To address this problem, as part of the ERC-funded research project iLABOUR, we have developed the \"Online Labour Index\" (OLI), an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics. The OLI has already had major international social impact by exposing the geographic and occupational divisions in the otherwise invisible online labour market." Report teaser: "The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy, which refers to work transacted fully digitally via websites and apps. The gig economy constitutes a new and rapidly growing form of non-standard work, which is already the main source of income for approximately 1% of the..."

**101003134 GHOSTWORK** - objective: "This on-demand work is offered and performed online, paid by the task, on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. Conceptualized as 'ghost work', this rapidly growing, platform-based work is largely unseen: workers are unable to speak with managers, do not get feedback, and lack labour protections. How do these specific work conditions influence ghost workers' well-being?"

**101028811 COGONU** - objective: "In response to the rise of a new labour governance regime in the platform economy, militant forms of worker mobilization have recently emerged across Europe... it maps all episodes of couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016 accounting for similarities and differences in terms of strategies, action repertoire, and mobilization capacity." Report summary: "The rise of digital labour and the platform economy has triggered a burgeoning public interest in the topic of technological innovation in the workplace. However, only a few research projects have explored the conditions of workers."

- **947806 iManage** (OUT) - "employment law has paid scant attention to the rise of algorithmic management: the increasingly pervasive reliance on monitoring technology and sophisticated algorithms to measure, control, and sanction workers... How can employment law respond to a world in which automation has not replaced workers - but their bosses?" The gig economy is named once as context; the study population is employees under algorithmic supervision, not people whose jobs arrive through an app.

record.text: Several EU projects set out to turn software that writes music by itself into something they could sell. How did they differ in what that software was meant to do for its intended users?
record.reference_answer: I2C8 turned the Lrn2Cre8 FET project's machine-learning work into a digital audio workstation plug-in for chord sequence generation, pitched to electronic musicians, producers and DJs as a 'musical sketchpad'; it deliberately stays small - predominantly sequences of up to eight chords - because its stated aim is to 'inspire' for composing, not to deliver complete compositions. AIVA, an AI that trained itself on 30,000+ classical music pieces, went the other way and offered content creators finished royalty-free soundtracks 'in the matter of seconds, and at the touch of a button', transitioning from a service to an embeddable Music Engine plus an API that lets third-party developers create hundreds of hours of soundtrack music, and it validated commercial feasibility by testing users' response and willingness to pay for the Music Engine public beta released in the second half of 2019. CALMUSgaming, from the Icelandic SME ErkiTónlist and built on its CALMUS technology, targeted computer games instead: its report says the software generates new background music as the game evolves, with minimal contribution from the composer, saving up to 90% of the time devoted to music composition, and the funded work was a feasibility study covering technical scope, markets and competition, a patent search and a 5-year financial forecast. FlowMachines, a PoC of the ERC Flow-Machines project, treated musical style itself as the asset to sell and set out to build a style manipulation prototype for the music synchronization business - music composed to be synchronized to existing media such as advertisements, movie music or video games - but its report concludes that 'Direct commercial exploitation of AI technologies per se is no longer a profitable route', that the team shifted to producing, distributing and monetizing content by the music industry's 'traditional means', and that they convinced top executives of a major music label to create a dedicated label specialized in the production and dissemination of music composed with AI technologies; on the legal side it catalogued the copyright issues in a report but 'considered that it was not worth addressing the issues raised by each copyright type'.
