record.text: Which projects study the workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces, such as couriers, drivers, or people paid task by task over the internet?
record.reference_answer: Eight projects study this workforce, in three groups. Fieldwork on who these workers are and what the work does to them: PLABOR established that platform-based gig work in Amsterdam, Berlin and New York City is predominantly migrant work and documents the new risks it creates; GHOSTWORK follows the people who clean, code and classify data for AI on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, who cannot speak with managers, get no feedback and lack labour protections; REsPecTMe collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries and 98 expert interviews across care, gig and creative work in eight European countries to measure the unpaid labour buried inside paid work. Measurement and standard-setting: iLABOUR analysed how online labour markets pull workers out of national frameworks such as employment law and collective bargaining and impose their own technologically enforced institutions; GIGSTATS turned its Online Labour Index into a public statistics tool for work transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps and used it to measure that workforce itself - roughly 60% growth over five years, its geographic and occupational divisions, and women's participation in it; FAIRWORK co-develops fair work principles and rates and ranks platforms against them. Regulation and collective action: PLUS studies AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber across seven European cities to produce a Chart for digital workers' rights plus taxation and regulation guidelines, and COGONU maps every episode of food delivery couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016.
record.notes: Seeds: candidate vector-43 supplied six ids from an ILIKE '%gig economy%' probe (833577, 837539, 838081, 875255, 890434, 947806); re-executed this session, still exactly those six. The probe was treated as a substring probe, not a gold set. GOLD (8): 639652 iLABOUR (online labour markets, their institutions and worker movements); 759776 PLABOR (on-demand labour platforms, migrant platform workers in Amsterdam/Berlin/NYC); 822638 PLUS (platform labour in seven cities, Deliveroo/Uber/Helpling/AirBnb); 833577 REsPecTMe (precariousness measured across care, gig and creative work, 414 biographical interviews); 838081 FAIRWORK (platform workers' pay and conditions, rating platforms); 875255 GIGSTATS (Online Labour Index measuring work transacted via websites and apps); 101003134 GHOSTWORK (Mechanical Turk microtask workers' well-being); 101028811 COGONU (food delivery couriers' mobilizations). IN/OUT CRITERION (added at the fix round, settles 875255 against 101022491): a project is IN if the app-mediated workforce is itself the object being characterised - who these workers are, where they are, what they earn, what conditions they face - whether characterised one worker at a time or only in aggregate; it is OUT if those workers appear only as an input, a channel or context in a study whose object is something else. 875255 GIGSTATS is IN on the aggregate side: its report summary states 'The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy', 'we made significant advances in measuring the global online workforce', 'our OLI data revealed that the online gig economy grew approximately 60% over the past 5 years' and 'We expanded the topical and geographical scope of the OLI to Russian- and Spanish-language online freelance markets and to measuring the participation of women in the online gig economy' - the measured object is that workforce, even though no worker is interviewed and the objective text is proof-of-concept tooling (Excel-export interface, a public-organisation partnership, policy reports, a funding roadmap). 101022491 stays OUT under the same criterion: its two stated objectives are 'Estimate how ride-hailing affects public transit' and 'Discover the mechanisms by which public transit and ride-hailing affect each other', measured by estimating 'the effect of new subway stations on Uber ridership' - the measured object is transit ridership and the city, and drivers are never characterised at all. RE-CHECK OF THE EXCLUDED SET UNDER THIS CRITERION (re-read this round): 715950 SHARE is the closest call - it does measure a workforce in aggregate ('how the solo self-employed are classified, measured, and represented', labour-force surveys plus cross-national ethnography) and its summary says solo self-employment 'concerns both high- and low-skilled jobs, as well as those performed through digital labour platforms' - but its population is defined by contractual status, not by getting work through an app, and platform-performed work is one clause inside it with no platform-specific finding reported; stays OUT. 822296 BEYOND4.0 likewise names 'the digitisation of work through the platform economy (also referred to as Uberisation)' as one of its two transformations, but what it characterises is jobs, skills, tax and welfare systems, not the workers; OUT. 890434 SOJUFOW characterises nothing empirically (normative political philosophy); 757395 WorkOD's object is a methodology for the contract for work; 639403 WORKANDHOME's object is home-based self-employment; 867466 YouthExistInTourism's object is young people in touristified places; 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina study employees under algorithmic supervision in conventional employment ('in each and every industry'); 895305 DweLinks studies short-term rental markets - all unchanged and all OUT. Nothing else in the excluded set is pulled in by the criterion. 870619 WorkYP OUT (adjudicated at the fix round; it was never in the pool, and the ILIKE '%gig economy%' probe could not reach it because it writes the hyphenated form): its subject is in-work poverty across seven countries, and 'casual/zero-hours/gig-economy workers' is the fourth of four Vulnerable and Underrepresented Persons clusters, named in one clause of the objective and of the summary; its report's workPerformed and finalResults report only legal and policy outputs (EU social citizenship, 'fair and adequate wages', 29 deliverables, two conferences) and no finding about app-mediated workers. That standard reads consistently against 833577 REsPecTMe, which is IN not because gig work is listed among its sectors but because it fielded it: 'we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries', 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, 98 expert interviews. OTHER DELIBERATE NEAR-MISSES, all read in full: 947806 iManage and 893888 Boss Ex Machina OUT - both study algorithmic monitoring and management of employees in conventional employment, not workers whose jobs come through apps; 890434 SOJUFOW OUT - normative political philosophy of labour-market justice, gig economy named only as one of three trends, no study of the workers; 757395 WorkOD OUT - labour-law methodology for contracting for work, gig-based work an instance explained; 715950 SHARE OUT - solo self-employment generally; 822296 BEYOND4.0 OUT - Industry 4.0 impacts on work broadly; 895305 DweLinks OUT - short-term rental markets, not workers; 867466 YouthExistInTourism OUT - tourism employment in Goa and Lisbon, 'gig economies' used loosely, not app-mediated; 101022491 ride-hailing OUT - estimates ride-hailing's effect on public transport ridership, not on drivers; 639403 WORKANDHOME OUT - home-based self-employment and businesses, digital platforms only a data source. PLATFORM BUILDERS, all OUT (they create such marketplaces, they do not study the work): 837539 Mercurius Connect ('a Gig economy marketplace' for radiotherapy dosimetrists), 837395 C2C4LMB/Gigstarter, 877557 WorkPilots, 761756 Part-up, 862780 TaxiDriver, 876581 SWIFTLY, 808366 TiMMi Transport, 720657 DynaHUBS, 674203 CAIN, 652511 CroDS, 759207 P2PMODELS, 739349 P2Property, 775417 P2PCS. evidence:
Per gold project, the passages that satisfy "workers who make a living from short jobs handed out through smartphone apps and online marketplaces".

**639652 iLABOUR** - report summary: "The 'gig economy' or 'platform economy' has emerged as a key theme in debates around digitalisation and the future of work. It can be defined as \"people using apps and websites, commonly known as platforms, to sell their labour\". The gig economy consists both of work that is transacted via platforms but delivered locally, and work that is transacted and delivered remotely over the Internet." Objective: "online labour markets that connect firms with knowledge and service workers around the world have grown up to 60% a year... An overlooked aspect of these markets is that they extricate workers and employers from national institutional frameworks, such as employment law and collective bargaining, and instead impose their own, technologically enforced institutions. For example, a leading marketplace recently instated a global minimum wage of 4.00 USD/h."

**759776 PLABOR** - report workPerformed: "So-called \"gig economy\" platforms in particular provide much needed income opportunities for people who have a distance to regular labor markets due to their legal status or gendered care duties at home. We have established that platform-based gig work is predominantly migrant work, given how relatively easy it is for (irregular) migrants to get started on a platform. Yet we also document how gig platforms introduce new risks and vuln[erabilities]". Objective: "determining how on-demand labor platforms distribute new opportunities and vulnerabilities for workers along gender, class, and racial lines... a cross-national comparative study that examines how platforms operate in three quickly growing and distinct tech hubs: Amsterdam, Berlin, and New York City."

**822638 PLUS** - report workPerformed: "a field work research on platform labour in terms of work organization, skills and social protections". Objective: "PLUS frames a ground-breaking grid of investigation that intertwines four disruptive platforms (AirBnb, Deliveroo, Helpling and Uber) and seven European cities (Barcelona, Berlin, Bologna, Lisbon, London, Paris, Tallinn)... in order to... produce outputs directly impacting on policy-making, market and welfare: innovative typologies of contracts, a Chart for digital workers' rights, taxation and regulation guidelines".

**833577 REsPecTMe** - report summary: "We collected 414 biographical interviews, 93 audio diaries, and 98 expert interviews across three work areas: creative, gig, and care work, in eight European countries." Report workPerformed: "we successfully collected data from workers and experts in care, gig, and creative sectors using biographical interviews and work diaries." Objective: "newly emerging on- and offline work in the gig economy for which people in paid work are not compensated or where it is used to access paid work."

**838081 FAIRWORK** - objective: "Millions of platform workers live all over the world: doing work that is outsourced via platforms or apps in the 'gig economy.' Workers tend to have little ability to negotiate wages or working conditions with the platforms that give them work... many workers have jobs characterized by long and irregular hours, low income, and high stress... It seeks to co-develop fair work principles with key stakeholders, develop methods to assess those principles, and ultimately rate and rank platforms against how they score against the fair work principles."

**875255 GIGSTATS** - objective: "existing economic statistics are not well suited to measuring work that is transacted entirely digitally via websites and apps (the so-called online gig economy). To address this problem, as part of the ERC-funded research project iLABOUR, we have developed the \"Online Labour Index\" (OLI), an online gig economy equivalent of conventional labour market statistics. The OLI has already had major international social impact by exposing the geographic and occupational divisions in the otherwise invisible online labour market." Report teaser: "The GIGSTATS project studied the online gig economy, which refers to work transacted fully digitally via websites and apps. The gig economy constitutes a new and rapidly growing form of non-standard work, which is already the main source of income for approximately 1% of the..."

**101003134 GHOSTWORK** - objective: "This on-demand work is offered and performed online, paid by the task, on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. Conceptualized as 'ghost work', this rapidly growing, platform-based work is largely unseen: workers are unable to speak with managers, do not get feedback, and lack labour protections. How do these specific work conditions influence ghost workers' well-being?"

**101028811 COGONU** - objective: "In response to the rise of a new labour governance regime in the platform economy, militant forms of worker mobilization have recently emerged across Europe... it maps all episodes of couriers' mobilizations across Europe since 2016 accounting for similarities and differences in terms of strategies, action repertoire, and mobilization capacity." record.text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
record.reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and reports that because 'particularly resourceful firms are able to carry their political demands to policymakers, interest representation might be skewed in their favor'; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States and, as delivered, focused on three policy fields - corporate taxation, inheritance taxation and wage bargaining - finding that the responsiveness of governments to business demands depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a policy maker's choice of environmental policy instrument; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: POWERSHIFTS finds that 'firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation' and that 'incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes'; MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy; GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries; EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how non-state actors including business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies and priorities between 1958 and 1992; EURECON studies the influence of non-state actors including commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making; and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.
record.notes: Seeds: PROSPER 842868 and LOBFRAM 657949 from the corpus-profile candidate (social sciences/political sciences bucket), read before the question existed; the question was composed from PROSPER's 'firms ... influence trade policymaking' and LOBFRAM's 'non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups'. Candidate drift check (first pass): the candidate's in-bucket lobbying cluster re-executes to 9 members, not 5; corpus-wide there are 17 projects with 'lobb' in project.objective and 84 with 'lobb' in objective or any report_text section, so the euroSciVoc fence was dropped and gold was built corpus-wide. GOLD RULE (tightened this pass): IN iff the project's own research, as stated in its objective or its published report sections, examines efforts to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making AND the influencing actor is identified in the project's own text as business, firms, corporate or industry. OUT: the project's own advocacy or dissemination; passing background mentions; an influence claim attributed only to a cited literature rather than to the project's own findings; influencers named only as lobbies, special interests, interest groups or lobbyists with no business identification; and the reverse direction (regulation acting on an industry). The tightened rule changed three cases this pass: CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 dropped from gold (its texts say 'lobbies' and 'powerful special interests', never business/firms/corporate/industry - the same ground on which CONSERVATION 683031 was already out); PARTICIPATE 948516 dropped from gold (its own delivered finding is the tax-price elasticity of corporate giving, and the influence claim 'corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics' is explicitly attributed to 'the recent literature on tax-exempt lobbying'); SPIKE 797989 adjudicated and named OUT (it studies the US lobbying industry itself - 'quantify the importance of lobbyist-client relationships' - and aims to inform 'the regulation of advocacy services', not business influence on policy). The four other previously disclosed weak members were re-run under the same rule and stay IN because each names a business actor in its own text: UneqDems 741538 ('the exercise of business power in switzerland'), IFDG 786587 ('us firms react more to increased competition from china by lobbying more'), GRIP-ARM 950056 ('how do state capacity, business power and organizational structure of domestic markets shape the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries?'), CORPORATOCRACY 865165 ('Business corporations exercise political power, both internally ... and externally (towards states, consumers and others)'). POWERSHIFTS 751843 added to gold: its own report finds 'Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits' and 'Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes', and its workPerformed reports that renewable energy communities build political coalitions 'most often with renewables companies and industry groups'. All 58 are OUT. The recurring patterns are the reverse direction, regulation pressuring an industry (GRAIL 638719, iLABOUR 639652, TyRec 672558, HEAT-R 697982, Auxilia 775737, Triboconditioning 823307, CLIMEX 851876, FinanceCC 885552, LAND GRIFFON 101004174); the project's own dissemination or advocacy (PV FINANCING 646554, progRESsHEAT 646573, SmartAct-2-3 650702, FloTEC 691916, InnoRenew CoE 739574, IFASA 744848, AQUA-FAANG 817923, RESTORE 820292, CASCADES 821010, SENSEI 847066, 5GMED 951947, EU-PolarNet 2 101003766); stakeholder or audience lists (SLALOM 644270, BeLEADFREE 691503, CineAF 891966); and false positives on device or process vocabulary ('pressure regulator': M-H70 826062, P200 876347; CO2 'capture': ACCSESS 101022487). Three S5 rows were read in full before rejection: MANAGLOBAL 823744 (local management practice and 'private companies' government' in African and Arab countries - corporate governance, not public policy), FASHION IN IR 886026 (the influence of French women's fashion on the American mass market and within the common market, not business influence on government policy), RECENT 823903 (beyond-5G wireless networks; the hit is an impact sentence about consortium companies and technical standards). S5 produced no new gold beyond POWERSHIFTS 751843, which the judge supplied. term_style paraphrase, recounted this pass by SQL over objective plus all report sections: 10 of the 16 gold texts carry a 'lobb' token as their key term (LOBFRAM, EFTA DEVELOPMENT, MILO, IFDG, MIGPSC, DIA, TRASC, BIZPOL, PROSPER, ClimActiv) and 6 do not (BUSWEL, EURECON, UneqDems, POWERSHIFTS, CORPORATOCRACY, GRIP-ARM), while the question uses none of that vocabulary, saying 'try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt'; consistent with the rank matrix, where only BUSWEL (lexical 8), PROSPER (lexical 13) and LOBFRAM (lexical 17) reach the lexical top-20 and the rest of the pooled gold arrives via dense/hybrid/rerank. Named near-misses left OUT: CITIZINGLOBAL 714905, PARTICIPATE 948516 and SPIKE 797989 (reasons above), REVEAL 725798 (resilience of private rule-making bodies, not efforts to shape government policy), TRADEPOWER 724107 (bargaining power of countries in trade negotiations), POLBUSNETWORKS 724501 (firm-politician favour networks and misallocation), CLIFF 101020082 ('fossil fuel vested interests are lobbying heavily' is scene-setting), Digital Good 804985 (one workPerformed bullet), IMPACT HAU 772544 (lobbyists named among ethnographic case sites), CONSERVATION 683031 (lobbyists unspecified, in a resource-conservation game-theory paper), ENERGY ETHICS 715146 ('the strong industry lobbies' as context), PmNC 832350 and DemocInChange 702134 and DEMSEC 639021 and CONSULTATIONEFFECTS 804288 (civil society or interest groups not identified as business), Dia-Pol 101028566 (activists), CitIndus 890615 and WELTECH 101033625 (background phrases), FEDCIT 740447 (lobbying by municipalities), PEMP 637662 (lobbying listed as a future application). Remaining doubt: GRIP-ARM 950056 and CORPORATOCRACY 865165 still rest mainly on their objectives - both are ongoing and their interim reports do not repeat the phrase - so they are the two members most exposed to a stricter report-only reading.

1. **842868 PROSPER** - "Politics of Rulemaking, Orchestration of Standards, and Private Economic Regulations". Objective: "PROSPER will primarily investigate the extent to which MNCs are able to orchestrate political mobilization of their subsidiaries for coordinated lobbying and impose rules and standards upon firms along their supply chains." Objective: "CPA comprises all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests." Report summary/teaser: "as the best resourced and often most effective lobby force business also play a very important and consequential role in politics" [lc]. Report workPerformed: "An eco-system perspective was applied to map interest, influencing strategies and expectations of different relevant stakeholder groups".
3. **834253 TRASC** - "Trade Agreements and Supply Chains". Objective: "I will examine how large corporations with international supply chains shape the content and political support for deep RTAs". Report workPerformed: "We also study how firm-level lobbying shapes the content of FTAs. The dataset provides information on firms' lobbying effort to influence deep trade policies (e.g., intellectual property rights, investment rules, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, labor and environmental regulations)". Report summary: "i examine how lobbying by large corporations affects rtas (the probability that they are ratified, as well as the provisions included in them) and ad duties" [lc].

Objective: "BUSWEL analyzes how the strategies and activities of business interest groups have contributed to these diverging outcomes. The project compares policy positions and strategies of business interest groups in five countries: Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria, and the United States." Report finalResults: "the focus of the project on government responsiveness toward business demands for tax cuts has moved our understanding of the impact of business interest groups on the politics of social inequality forward" [lc].
5. **748066 MILO** - "Mining, lobbying and efficient environmental policy". Objective: "investigate the optimal environmental policy of the mining sector with a special emphasis on ... the choice of policy instruments under lobbying ... new insights on the formation of lobby groups and policy instruments". Report summary: "the polluters can influence the policy maker's instrument choice ... by focusing on the firms' incentives to join the lobby group and by investigating the consequences of this to instrument choice" [lc]. 8. **657949 LOBFRAM** - "Lobbying and framing in foreign policy". 9. **786587 IFDG** - "Innovation, firm dynamics and growth" (delivered strand). Report workPerformed: "the project on the impact of foreign competition on firms lobbying behavior has first consisted in collecting the datasets on lobbying expenditures, firms' financial information, patents and trade flows from different sources" [lc]. Report summary: "a fourth study looks at the extent to which us firms react more to increased competition from china by lobbying more" [lc]. Report finalResults: "we are also the first to focus on the indirect effect a shock in foreign competition can trigger in firms' lobbying expenses" [lc].
10. **798769 MIGPSC** - report summary states the research question: "how do private security actors and defence industry shape the european migration management policy inside and outside the eu borders?" [lc]; a second report passage: "rly true internally, at the policy-making level (essentially through lobbying), and externally, in particular in the mediterranean region" [lc].

Objective: "The project also intends to encourage the study of the critical influence of non-EEC and non-state actors and factors on the European decision-making level. 13. **714905 CITIZINGLOBAL** - "Citizens, Institutions and Globalization". Report teaser/summary open with "Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits" and "Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes". record.text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
record.reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and reports that because 'particularly resourceful firms are able to carry their political demands to policymakers, interest representation might be skewed in their favor'; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States and, as delivered, focused on three policy fields - corporate taxation, inheritance taxation and wage bargaining - finding that the responsiveness of governments to business demands depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a policy maker's choice of environmental policy instrument; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: POWERSHIFTS finds that 'firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation' and that 'incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes'; MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy; GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries; EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how non-state actors including business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies and priorities between 1958 and 1992; EURECON studies the influence of non-state actors including commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making; and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.
record.notes: Seeds: PROSPER 842868 and LOBFRAM 657949 from the corpus-profile candidate (social sciences/political sciences bucket), read before the question existed; the question was composed from PROSPER's 'firms ... influence trade policymaking' and LOBFRAM's 'non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups'. Candidate drift check (first pass): the candidate's in-bucket lobbying cluster re-executes to 9 members, not 5; corpus-wide there are 17 projects with 'lobb' in project.objective and 84 with 'lobb' in objective or any report_text section, so the euroSciVoc fence was dropped and gold was built corpus-wide. GOLD RULE (tightened this pass): IN iff the project's own research, as stated in its objective or its published report sections, examines efforts to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making AND the influencing actor is identified in the project's own text as business, firms, corporate or industry. OUT: the project's own advocacy or dissemination; passing background mentions; an influence claim attributed only to a cited literature rather than to the project's own findings; influencers named only as lobbies, special interests, interest groups or lobbyists with no business identification; and the reverse direction (regulation acting on an industry). The tightened rule changed three cases this pass: CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 dropped from gold (its texts say 'lobbies' and 'powerful special interests', never business/firms/corporate/industry - the same ground on which CONSERVATION 683031 was already out); PARTICIPATE 948516 dropped from gold (its own delivered finding is the tax-price elasticity of corporate giving, and the influence claim 'corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics' is explicitly attributed to 'the recent literature on tax-exempt lobbying'); SPIKE 797989 adjudicated and named OUT (it studies the US lobbying industry itself - 'quantify the importance of lobbyist-client relationships' - and aims to inform 'the regulation of advocacy services', not business influence on policy). The four other previously disclosed weak members were re-run under the same rule and stay IN because each names a business actor in its own text: UneqDems 741538 ('the exercise of business power in switzerland'), IFDG 786587 ('us firms react more to increased competition from china by lobbying more'), GRIP-ARM 950056 ('how do state capacity, business power and organizational structure of domestic markets shape the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries?'), CORPORATOCRACY 865165 ('Business corporations exercise political power, both internally ... and externally (towards states, consumers and others)'). POWERSHIFTS 751843 added to gold: its own report finds 'Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits' and 'Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes', and its workPerformed reports that renewable energy communities build political coalitions 'most often with renewables companies and industry groups'. Objective: "PROSPER will primarily investigate the extent to which MNCs are able to orchestrate political mobilization of their subsidiaries for coordinated lobbying and impose rules and standards upon firms along their supply chains." Report summary: "examine the role of private international actors, i.e., firms, which mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union (EU)." findings.claim: POWERSHIFTS 751843 (Shifting political power: the nature and consequences of distributed renewable energy transitions) studies exactly what the question asks - how energy firms and industry groups exercise influence over energy policy - and it appears in neither gold_project_ids nor the 38 pooled rejections nor the named near-miss list, so it was never adjudicated.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([751843]). Report teaser/summary open with "Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits" and "Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes". The objective's research questions are to examine the conditions leading to shifts in political power, assess the mechanisms, and identify the consequences, with influence channels named as "changes in access to policy makers, media influence" and outcomes as "contested carbon targets, renewable energy subsidies". workPerformed: "RECs are increasingly adept at building political coalitions to increase their policy impact. This is most often with renewables companies and industry groups". That meets the drafter's own IN rule and is not the project's own advocacy nor a background mention. It reached dense rank 8 / hybrid 12 / hybrid_rerank 15 on the critic's reformulation, so a system under test can retrieve it and would be scored wrong for doing so. Why the sweeps could not find it, executed: regexp over objective+all report sections for 751843 returned no 'lobb' token anywhere (so S1 and S2 were structurally blind to it) and no match on the actor-first proximity order, only on the reverse policy-first order. The blind spot is directional and applies corpus-wide, so this is a mechanism, not a single slip: further members may be reachable only by opposed/resisted/pushed-for verbs and policy-first phrasing.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - adding 751843 makes gold 18 and leaves the cell at L3, so level and subtype are untouched; the reference answer would need one clause for it. The more durable edit is to re-run the completeness sweep with the proximity pattern in BOTH orders and with an opposition/advocacy verb set (oppose, resist, block, push for, campaign, advocate, press) before the gold is fixed, since the same gap that hid this project is still open.
findings.ruling_why: The critic read 751843 POWERSHIFTS in full and showed it satisfies the drafter's own stated IN rule ("Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes", "RECs ... building political coalitions ... with renewables companies and industry groups"), it appears nowhere in gold, the 38 pooled rejections or the near-miss list, and it retrieves at dense 8 / hybrid 12 / rerank 15 - so a system that finds it is scored wrong; the drafter's four sweeps could not refute this because all of them were keyed on the `lobb` stem or on actor-first word order, which 751843 matches in neither.

findings.claim: PARTICIPATE 948516 is a campaign-finance and charitable-giving project; nothing it researches examines companies trying to influence the policies or regulations governments adopt, and the one sentence the draft relies on describes a literature the project contributes to, not its own finding.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([948516]), full summary/workPerformed/finalResults. The stated goal is "the study of campaign finance, information and influence" through the motives behind small campaign contributions, the tax-price elasticity of political donations, political selection and media exposure. The six workPerformed items are Small Campaign Donors, Is Charitable Giving Political?, The Far-Right Donation Gap, a Political Inequality review, a tax-treatment survey experiment, and Tax Incentives or Political Motivations? Evidence from Corporate Contribution, which estimates the tax price elasticity of corporate donations. The draft's supporting quote reads in full: "the working paper ... contributes to the literature by providing the first estimation of the tax price elasticity of corporate giving ... Furthermore, we also contribute to the recent literature on 'tax-exempt lobbying' that shows that, at least in the U.S. context, corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics." The influence claim belongs to the cited literature, and it is "influence politics", not policies or regulations governments adopt. This is the same weight of support the drafter itself rejected for CLIFF 101020082 and PEMP 637662.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - dropping 948516 leaves gold at 16 and the cell at L3, and removes one sentence from the reference answer. If kept, the record should say which of its own findings - not which cited literature - examines business influence on policy.
findings.ruling_why: On PARTICIPATE 948516 the critic quoted the drafter's own supporting sentence in full and it attributes the influence claim to a literature the project contributes to ("we also contribute to the recent literature on 'tax-exempt lobbying' that shows ..."), not to the project's own research, which is the same weight of support the drafter itself ruled insufficient for CLIFF 101020082 and PEMP 637662.

findings.claim: The membership rule is applied in two directions at once. CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 is IN although its influencers are never identified as business, while CONSERVATION 683031 was put OUT for exactly "lobbyists unspecified", and SPIKE 797989 - which turns up in the same 17-row S1 sweep and is in the same category - is adjudicated nowhere in the package.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([714905]): the objective says "how lobbies can raise [protectionism] by manipulating information ... lobbies can raise protection by channeling information to insiders"; the report summary says "powerful special interests can capture government decisions when citizens are poorly informed". Neither business, firm, corporate nor industry appears as the influencing actor anywhere in its text - the drafter discloses this itself. The draft's stated OUT rule is "interest groups not identified as business", applied to CONSERVATION 683031, DEMSEC 639021 and CONSULTATIONEFFECTS 804288. The critic re-ran S1 independently: regexp_matches(lower(objective),'\blobb') returns exactly 17 rows, reproducing the drafter's count. Four are gold (657949, 714905, 748066, 842868), four are named rejections (637662, 702134, 721916, 740447), nine are unmentioned. Eight of those nine are clean excludes under the stated rule (uP_running 691748, AB-Prevention 717273, IFASA 744848, SWEETENED HEARTS 898829 are the project's own advocacy; EuroAgeism 764632 trains lobbyists; N-T-AUTONOMY 758015 and TGL 845118 are minority groups and NGOs; INTERMESTIC 659369 is parliaments and unspecified interest groups). The ninth, SPIKE 797989, is not: its objective is "I use data from the US lobbying industry ... I will quantify the importance of lobbyist-client relationships", aiming to "inform the policy debate on how to reduce political corruption and improve the quality of regulation in advocacy services", and its workPerformed reports a unique dataset on lobbying efforts. Its influencers are unspecified lobbyists - the CITIZINGLOBAL situation exactly. So one of the two treatments is wrong; the record cannot support both.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY, and either direction keeps the cell at L3 - tighten the rule to "the influencing actor is identified as business in the project's own text" and drop 714905 (gold 16), or widen it to organised private interests and adjudicate 797989 and 683031 on the record. Note this interacts with the MISSED-GOLD finding: that one adds a member, this and the PARTICIPATE finding each remove one.
findings.ruling_why: On CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 the critic independently reproduced the 17-row S1 sweep and showed the membership rule runs in two directions at once: 714905 is IN with unspecified "lobbies" and "powerful special interests" while CONSERVATION 683031 is OUT for exactly "lobbyists unspecified" and SPIKE 797989, the same case, is adjudicated nowhere - so the gold set does not survive independent re-derivation from the rule the record states.

findings.claim: The reference answer states BUSWEL's three policy fields as corporate tax cuts, payroll tax cuts and deregulation of employment protection. That is the proposal's plan; BUSWEL's own report says the delivered fields were corporate taxation, inheritance taxation and wage bargaining, so a system that summarises the project from its results would be scored against a reference its evidence contradicts.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([705677]). Objective: "The project focuses on three policy issues that are assumed to have an effect on social redistribution: corporate tax cuts, payroll tax cuts and deregulation of employment protection." Report summary: "This project investigated the contribution of political activities by business interest groups ... The project focused on three policy fields: corporate taxation, inheritance taxation, and wage bargaining", with the two worked examples being the study of wage bargaining and the study of reforms in corporate taxes and inheritance taxes. Payroll tax and employment protection appear nowhere in the report. The second half of the reference's BUSWEL sentence is clean. For completeness the critic checked two other specific reference claims and both hold verbatim - PROSPER 842868 finalResults contains both "the relative decline of sector associations" and "the largest and most productive firms - i.e. multinationals - dominate the political scene", and MILO 748066 workPerformed contains "the choice between a quantity instrument (emission limit) and a price instrument (emission tax) when the formation of the lobby group is endogenous".
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - one bounded edit to the reference clause: either name the delivered fields (corporate taxation, inheritance taxation, wage bargaining) or say "five countries, on tax and bargaining policy" without enumerating. The rest of the answer is untouched.

record.text: Which EU-funded projects study how companies and business groups try to influence the policies and regulations that governments adopt?
record.reference_answer: EU-funded research on this question sits mostly in political economy, and it covers both who does the influencing and what it achieves. Several projects put firms at the centre of trade rule-making: PROSPER studies firms that 'mobilize politically across global trade networks and influence trade policymaking in the European Union' and reports that because 'particularly resourceful firms are able to carry their political demands to policymakers, interest representation might be skewed in their favor'; TRASC builds a firm-level dataset of lobbying on the ratification and content of free trade agreements and on antidumping measures; DIA reports that the effect of industry lobbying on international rule-making depends on whether industries across countries share common or conflicting interests. Other projects work on domestic policy: BUSWEL compares the policy positions and strategies of business interest groups in Denmark, Sweden, Germany, Austria and the United States and, as delivered, focused on three policy fields - corporate taxation, inheritance taxation and wage bargaining - finding that the responsiveness of governments to business demands depends on the policy at hand and on the types of firms represented; MILO models how polluting firms' incentives to join a lobby group shape a policy maker's choice of environmental policy instrument; BIZPOL maps corporate political activity, 'all non-market activities by companies when they engage with governments and policy-making more broadly to advance their interests'. The set reaches further sectors and periods: POWERSHIFTS finds that 'firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation' and that 'incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes'; MIGPSC asks how private security actors and the defence industry shape European migration management policy; GRIP-ARM asks how business power shapes the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries; EFTA DEVELOPMENT traces how non-state actors including business lobby groups shaped EFTA's policies and priorities between 1958 and 1992; EURECON studies the influence of non-state actors including commercial banks and big business on European economic decision-making; and ClimActiv and CORPORATOCRACY treat corporate lobbying and corporate political power as questions of democratic legitimacy rather than of measurement.
record.notes: Seeds: PROSPER 842868 and LOBFRAM 657949 from the corpus-profile candidate (social sciences/political sciences bucket), read before the question existed; the question was composed from PROSPER's 'firms ... influence trade policymaking' and LOBFRAM's 'non-state actors (NSAs), such as business groups'. Candidate drift check (first pass): the candidate's in-bucket lobbying cluster re-executes to 9 members, not 5; corpus-wide there are 17 projects with 'lobb' in project.objective and 84 with 'lobb' in objective or any report_text section, so the euroSciVoc fence was dropped and gold was built corpus-wide. GOLD RULE (tightened this pass): IN iff the project's own research, as stated in its objective or its published report sections, examines efforts to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making AND the influencing actor is identified in the project's own text as business, firms, corporate or industry. OUT: the project's own advocacy or dissemination; passing background mentions; an influence claim attributed only to a cited literature rather than to the project's own findings; influencers named only as lobbies, special interests, interest groups or lobbyists with no business identification; and the reverse direction (regulation acting on an industry). The tightened rule changed three cases this pass: CITIZINGLOBAL 714905 dropped from gold (its texts say 'lobbies' and 'powerful special interests', never business/firms/corporate/industry - the same ground on which CONSERVATION 683031 was already out); PARTICIPATE 948516 dropped from gold (its own delivered finding is the tax-price elasticity of corporate giving, and the influence claim 'corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics' is explicitly attributed to 'the recent literature on tax-exempt lobbying'); SPIKE 797989 adjudicated and named OUT (it studies the US lobbying industry itself - 'quantify the importance of lobbyist-client relationships' - and aims to inform 'the regulation of advocacy services', not business influence on policy). The four other previously disclosed weak members were re-run under the same rule and stay IN because each names a business actor in its own text: UneqDems 741538 ('the exercise of business power in switzerland'), IFDG 786587 ('us firms react more to increased competition from china by lobbying more'), GRIP-ARM 950056 ('how do state capacity, business power and organizational structure of domestic markets shape the design of industrial policies in resource-rich countries?'), CORPORATOCRACY 865165 ('Business corporations exercise political power, both internally ... and externally (towards states, consumers and others)'). POWERSHIFTS 751843 added to gold: its own report finds 'Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits' and 'Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes', and its workPerformed reports that renewable energy communities build political coalitions 'most often with renewables companies and industry groups'. Pooling arithmetic: 43 candidates were pooled across the four conditions at k=20; 5 of them are gold (BUSWEL 705677, PROSPER 842868, TRASC 834253, BIZPOL 840978, LOBFRAM 657949) and the other 38 were rejected, so pooled_candidate_count 43 = 5 pooled-and-accepted + rejected_count 38. The `accepted` field carries all 16 gold ids because the brief requires accepted == gold_project_ids; the 11 gold that are not in that 5 were never in the pool at all - they were found by the SQL completeness sweeps below. findings.claim: POWERSHIFTS 751843 (Shifting political power: the nature and consequences of distributed renewable energy transitions) studies exactly what the question asks - how energy firms and industry groups exercise influence over energy policy - and it appears in neither gold_project_ids nor the 38 pooled rejections nor the named near-miss list, so it was never adjudicated.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([751843]). Report teaser/summary open with "Firms in centralised systems have actively opposed policies that facilitate increased decentralisation as they seek to protect their market shares and profits" and "Incumbent generators wield significant influence over energy policy processes". The objective's research questions are to examine the conditions leading to shifts in political power, assess the mechanisms, and identify the consequences, with influence channels named as "changes in access to policy makers, media influence" and outcomes as "contested carbon targets, renewable energy subsidies". workPerformed: "RECs are increasingly adept at building political coalitions to increase their policy impact. This is most often with renewables companies and industry groups". That meets the drafter's own IN rule and is not the project's own advocacy nor a background mention. It reached dense rank 8 / hybrid 12 / hybrid_rerank 15 on the critic's reformulation, so a system under test can retrieve it and would be scored wrong for doing so. Why the sweeps could not find it, executed: regexp over objective+all report sections for 751843 returned no 'lobb' token anywhere (so S1 and S2 were structurally blind to it) and no match on the actor-first proximity order, only on the reverse policy-first order. The blind spot is directional and applies corpus-wide, so this is a mechanism, not a single slip: further members may be reachable only by opposed/resisted/pushed-for verbs and policy-first phrasing.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - adding 751843 makes gold 18 and leaves the cell at L3, so level and subtype are untouched; the reference answer would need one clause for it. The more durable edit is to re-run the completeness sweep with the proximity pattern in BOTH orders and with an opposition/advocacy verb set (oppose, resist, block, push for, campaign, advocate, press) before the gold is fixed, since the same gap that hid this project is still open.

findings.claim: PARTICIPATE 948516 is a campaign-finance and charitable-giving project; nothing it researches examines companies trying to influence the policies or regulations governments adopt, and the one sentence the draft relies on describes a literature the project contributes to, not its own finding.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([948516]), full summary/workPerformed/finalResults. The stated goal is "the study of campaign finance, information and influence" through the motives behind small campaign contributions, the tax-price elasticity of political donations, political selection and media exposure. The six workPerformed items are Small Campaign Donors, Is Charitable Giving Political?, The Far-Right Donation Gap, a Political Inequality review, a tax-treatment survey experiment, and Tax Incentives or Political Motivations? The draft's supporting quote reads in full: "the working paper ... contributes to the literature by providing the first estimation of the tax price elasticity of corporate giving ... Furthermore, we also contribute to the recent literature on 'tax-exempt lobbying' that shows that, at least in the U.S. context, corporations sometimes use giving as a means to influence politics." The influence claim belongs to the cited literature, and it is "influence politics", not policies or regulations governments adopt. The critic's own pooled runs retrieved gold members (CORPORATOCRACY at rank 1 in three conditions) that the drafter's pooling never saw.

findings.claim: SEEGROW 895519 (Southeast Europe's emerging growth advocates) is a defensible OUT but is unnamed anywhere in the package.
findings.evidence: Its objective says its key aim is "to understand the extent to which these small economic agents are contributing to the reshaping of the rules of economic governance from the bottom-up in the context of state capture", which is firms reshaping rules, though its delivered work is about SME exports, ICT and spatial inequality rather than efforts directed at government. Read in full this session; the critic agrees with excluding it and notes only that it is the kind of case a reader would expect the near-miss list to name.

findings.claim: The tightened rule has two legs - the project's own research examines efforts to influence public policy, regulation or rule-making, AND the influencing actor is named as business, firms, corporate or industry. CORPORATOCRACY 865165 passes the second and fails the first: it is a political-philosophy project on whether corporate power is legitimate, and none of its five delivered subprojects examines corporations trying to influence what governments adopt. This is the same gap on which CITIZINGLOBAL and PARTICIPATE were removed this round.
findings.evidence: get_project_text([865165]), full objective and all report sections, untruncated. The objective's business sentence is "Business corporations exercise political power, both internally (towards their employees) and externally (towards states, consumers and others)", and its stated aim is "to determine the conditions that underpin the legitimacy of corporate political power" through three legitimacy conditions. The report's workPerformed enumerates the five subprojects: the corporate constitution, corporate democracy (workplace democracy, the Berlin expropriation movement, strikes), social justice (corporate responsibility for structural injustices, class-action lawsuits), transnational corporations (the multinational firm's effects on the freedom of sovereign political communities, value extraction), and the theory of the firm (the state/firm analogy, worker resistance, democratising social media corporations, antitrust). Lobbying, policy influence, rule-making and legislation appear nowhere. An independent span test over objective plus all four report sections for all 16 gold - regexp_matches(lower(...), '(influenc|lobb|shape|shaping|press|oppos)[a-z]*.{0,60}(polic|regulat|legislat|rule-?making)') - returns true for 14 and false for exactly two: BUSWEL 705677 and CORPORATOCRACY 865165. BUSWEL's false is a phrasing artefact (its objective states "BUSWEL analyzes how the strategies and activities of business interest groups have contributed to these diverging outcomes ... to identify the impact of these differences on the differing trajectories of policy change"). CORPORATOCRACY has no equivalent phrasing anywhere, which the full read confirms. The drafter's own recorded doubt frames this as the report not repeating the objective's phrase; the sharper problem is that the objective's phrase itself - political power exercised "towards states, consumers and others" - is not an effort to influence adopted policy.
findings.fix_direction: ADVISORY - dropping 865165 leaves gold at 15, still vector L3, and removes one half-clause from the reference's closing sentence; ClimActiv 101024225 carries that sentence on its own and is solid. The alternative bounded edit is to widen the rule's first leg to admit projects about corporate political power in general, but that reopens CITIZINGLOBAL, so the two cannot both stand as they are. Which of the two costs less is the judge's call.
findings.ruling_why: Real and accepted: the critic read 865165 CORPORATOCRACY's objective and all report sections untruncated, its five delivered subprojects contain no study of efforts to shape adopted policy, and its span test over all 16 gold isolates it and BUSWEL alone, with BUSWEL's miss shown to be a phrasing artefact - but this is a one-member periphery dispute in a 16-member survey whose level is unmoved at 16, 15 or 14, so it rides into the report as a disclosed note rather than a defect that changes what the cell measures. It is NOT the round-1 defect surviving: the round-1 GOLD-WRONG findings were an inconsistency in the ACTOR leg of the rule, that leg is now coherent and 865165 passes it, and the critic's evenness test in the excluded direction reached nothing new.

The rule as written keeps it in; a reader re-deriving the gold should expect to argue about it.

judge_decisions.rationale: Every upheld finding lands on the gold set and the reference, not on what the question asks or on the cell it sits in: the question text is a natural lay paraphrase of vocabulary 12 of the 17 gold texts own, the critic raised no discrimination finding, and |gold| moves at most from 17 to 16-18, which is L3 survey under every combination. What is broken is scoring accuracy inside that cell - one satisfying project that a system can retrieve and be punished for, two members held to a rule the record applies inconsistently, and a reference clause that contradicts its own project's report. That is a bounded edit to gold, notes and the reference answer with the question text untouched, so it does not force re-verification of the pooling, the rank matrix or term_style, and it is the fix the judge expects to land. No stop rule fires: this candidate has had no fix round, no class has killed two candidates here (candidate 0 died on AMBIGUOUS-READING), and one pass remains.

The level is insensitive to the entire zone of disagreement - gold at 16, at 15 without CORPORATOCRACY, or at the 14 of the strictest report-only reading the drafter itself names, is vector L3 survey every time and nowhere near the floor of 5 - so nothing surviving can move the cell, which is exactly the difference from candidate 0, where the boundary dispute chose the level. The HIGH that could have produced a wrong finding is closed by execution: S5 ran in both word orders with the widened verb set, 58 rows, not truncated, all adjudicated OUT, so POWERSHIFTS was the only project in the blind spot and it is now gold. The surviving MID runs in the benign direction - CORPORATOCRACY reaches rank 1 in three of four conditions on the critic's own reformulation, so keeping it in gold does not differentially punish the systems that did best the way a missed member does - and the record discloses it by name for the promote-time veto. The fix took and the record shows it: four of four round-1 findings verified resolved, the evenness test in the excluded direction returned nothing new over 10 fully read rows, and the critic's own full re-read of the eleven gold members it had never checked lands 14 of 16 clean on both legs, which is what the brief means by gold surviving independent re-derivation. The two LOW notes about the reference are recorded as notes only, since the critic states the rewritten clauses are accurate and nothing is broken.

evidence_carried_forward: evidence_carried_forward: (a) the pooled rank matrix and the 38 pooled rejections - not re-run, because no retrieval call was made this round and nothing in the edit changes what the four conditions returned at k=20 against index be84cbad9182; (b) the S1-S4 sweep counts (17 / 67 / 29 / 7 rows) - not re-run, because S5 is additive and its exclusion list already contains every project those sweeps adjudicated; (c) the verbatim satisfying passages for the twelve gold members other than POWERSHIFTS and BUSWEL - not re-pulled in full, though the four contested ones were re-adjudicated against SQL-extracted spans quoted in the evidence. The critic should re-measure all three.
